item.title: An Open Server, an Exposed Toolkit Inside a Viva Aerobus-Linked Intrusion
item.description:
An attacker's unauthenticated staging server exposed a full MSSQL post-exploitation toolkit linked to a Viva Aerobus-side intrusion, giving defenders a rare window into the workflow while simultaneously creating a secondary breach risk.
Key findings:
- The attacker staging server at 151.243.232[.]123 was left fully open to the internet with no authentication between September 25-29, 2026. At 16:20 on September 25, a victim-side MSSQL server pulled a payload from it. By 16:21, unrelated external hosts were already enumerating its exposed loot directories, and by 18:04 additional hosts were retrieving post-exploitation tooling directly. The attacker's infrastructure failure became its own secondary breach event within two hours of first use.
- Execution flowed entirely through xp_cmdshell on a compromised SQL Server instance, running T1059.001 encoded PowerShell and T1059.003 Windows Command Shell commands under the SQL Server service account. File exfiltration (T1041) bypassed conventional C2 by reading files, chunking them, Base64-encoding the content, and returning it through MSSQL query output, using the existing SQL execution channel as the data-transfer path.
- The exposed server held 17 named post-exploitation tools across credential dumping (chrome_dump.ps1, cred_dump.ps1, cred_enum.ps1), SQL credential spraying (sqlspray.ps1, mssqltest.ps1), file transfer (exfil[.]py, upload[.]py), and Windows Credential Manager or Vault access (vault.cmd, vtest.ps1). Loot directories contained Mimikatz output (T1003), DPAPI-protected saved-password material, and SSMS connection history (T1555), the last of which functions as a ready-made target map for follow-on SQL and SMB credential reuse (T1021). Configuration and source-code files containing SQL, OAuth, mail, SFTP, and payment integration references were also collected (T1552.001).
- Three tool hashes are confirmed in the public IOC set: exfil[.]py (c38f49ba68b891bb476510704cddf080798f3c70075e2a517e98e04e833f64fa), upload[.]py (33aeaaa3d57b7785ef2be5b8ccd39d534b8af50e0cd32a5036fdb64601a52fc9), sqlspray.ps1 (8b6c53e3d57b4c3049f3d0765a44d9a52feb6af78f1eaa5aff19daf1b9665998). The attacker working directory is C:\Windows\Temp\artex. ThreatMon confirms no evidence of successful lateral movement or sensitive passenger or payment data exfiltration, but withheld victim-specific credential material from the public release.
Defenders: search historical network telemetry for connections to 151.243.232[.]123 and scan endpoints for the three published hashes and the path C:\Windows\Temp\artex. In SQL Server environments, treat any unexpected xp_cmdshell activation, particularly cmd.exe or PowerShell spawning under the SQL Server service account or encoded command strings in query logs, as a high-priority investigation. Treat SSMS connection history and saved-password material as credential-adjacent artifacts requiring the same protection as credentials themselves. Any secrets confirmed to have reached this infrastructure should be rotated now regardless of observed downstream abuse. Full IOC set and ATT&CK mapping are in the ThreatMon report.

item.title: MSP360 RMM Abused in Phishing Campaigns to Deploy ScreenConnect
item.description:
Unattributed phishing campaigns abused legitimate MSP360 RMM software across multiple industries in July 2026 to deploy ScreenConnect as a redundant backdoor, enabling credential theft while blending into normal IT activity.
Key findings:
- The lure infrastructure was broad and rotated quickly. Phishing emails drove victims to attacker-controlled pages mimicking document portals, Adobe Reader, Zoom, Google Meet, DHL notices, SSA[.]GOV statements, and e-card RSVPs. Malicious installers were hosted across Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, GitLab, and Supabase, making domain-based blocking unreliable. The core payload was the same signed MSP360 RMM v2.5.0.67 binary regardless of lure theme: SHA256 108ef7e628d7a20bd6241a5b57149e27a6061f467123eb64061975559f8f73dc, SHA1 f34330d4c6e0aa978dc3af40360c14b31ad51127.
- The installer required UAC elevation to succeed: without it, no services or persistence were created. When approved, it logged two events through eventcreate.exe under the source "MSP360 RMM Agent installer" ("Begin installation" and "End installation. MSP360 de Success."), dropped components to C:\Program Files\RMM Agent, registered RMM.Agent.exe and RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe as services, wrote Registry autorun entries for tray apps, and opened a firewall rule allowing inbound UDP to RMM.Agent.exe on port 48678. The UAC prompt is the clearest early chokepoint to monitor or block.
- RMM.Agent.exe then spawned PowerShell, changed the execution policy, and used Invoke-WebRequest to pull ClientSetup.msi from actor infrastructure. Msiexec.exe ran it silently (/qn), registering ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe and ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe as a second independent remote access channel. The parent-child chain of RMM.Agent.exe > PowerShell > msiexec.exe is a high-fidelity process tree to hunt.
- ScreenConnect's RunFile feature staged and executed at least 25 named tools in C:\Users\%user%\OneDrive\Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp\ and C:\Users\%user%\Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp. Tools included WebBrowserPassView.exe, WebBrowserBookmarksView.exe, WindowsSecurity_Password.exe, WindowsPassKey.exe, Passwords.EXE, DefenderControl.exe, DefenderDT.exe, SCHider.exe, HideMouseApp.dll, HideFromControlPanel.exe, and PhoneLinkPrompt.exe. Names deliberately mimicked Windows, Defender, and Phone Link components to suppress analyst attention. A separate July cluster used FaronicsDeployAgent.exe in the same role as MSP360. Microsoft has not attributed either campaign.
Hunt for RMM.Agent.exe or RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe service registrations outside your approved toolset, the eventcreate.exe source "MSP360 RMM Agent installer" in the Application event log, and any process spawned from ScreenConnect writing executables to the ScreenConnect\Temp paths listed above. For credential exposure, check those Temp directories and browser credential store access by non-browser processes. Full IOC list and detection guidance are in the report.

item.title: Citrix NetScaler Post-Exploitation Payload Creates Superuser, Maps Web Shell to CSS-Like URLs
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771 (CVSS 9.5) actively exploited in the wild against Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, with post-exploitation chains creating superuser accounts, deploying disguised web shells, and exfiltrating full appliance configs.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88771 is a pre-authentication command injection flaw requiring no credentials. LevelBlue's THOR team identified exploitation activity across multiple customer environments, with attacker-controlled authentication strings containing "pitboss" and "NSPPE" as consistent markers in NetScaler auth logs. Separately, CVE-2026-88772 has been used to deliver PHP web shells (WHIPSHOT) and a Python tunneler named SLAPSHOT, per Mandiant and Google GTIG, with dozens of organizations already impacted.
- The Perl post-exploitation payload "update_c08937.pl" (retrieved from 64.94.85[.]67:443/update_c08937_08937.pl) is particularly aggressive: it modifies /flash/nsconfig/ns.conf to create a local account named "sec_monitor" with superuser role, archives the entire /flash/nsconfig directory to /tmp/update_result_3567cs.tgz, exfiltrates it to the same C2, then deletes the archive and wipes itself to reduce forensic footprint on disk.
- The web shell is written to /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/.local_journal, with /etc/httpd.conf modified to enable PHP execution and map the shell to URLs styled as legitimate NetScaler CSS resources. The permissions on /bin/sh are set to 6555 (SUID). This camouflage makes passive URL-based detection unreliable; defenders should be hashing and comparing /etc/httpd.conf against a known-good baseline and auditing unexpected SUID binaries.
- A Python reverse shell ("main[.]py", pulled from 23.27.143[.]20:9000/main.py) beacons outbound over TCP 443 to 45.141.21[.]130 and kills processes associated with /var/python/bin/customsnmpd. The "lula" payload was fetched from 31.56.197[.]72:9090/lula. Curl and wget activity retrieving these payloads from external IPs are your earliest post-exploitation signals in NetScaler logs.
- The Dutch 🇳🇱 NCSC pre-notified organizations and urged appliance shutdown, indicating active in-the-wild exploitation with confirmed impact before public disclosure. Attribution remains unknown at this time.
Responder action: Check /flash/nsconfig/ns.conf for the "sec_monitor" account and any unfamiliar local accounts with superuser role. Audit /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/ for unexpected files, especially hidden-name PHP files. Review /etc/httpd.conf for unauthorized rewrites pointing to CSS-like URL paths. Pull NetScaler auth logs and grep for "pitboss" and "NSPPE" strings as exploitation indicators. Verify /bin/sh permissions and check for outbound connections to the listed C2 IPs. IOCs are in the LevelBlue report.

item.title: Defender Exclusion Abuse: How Attackers Hide Malware from MDAV
item.description:
Attackers are abusing Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusions to blind AV scans, with a hidden registry key that can conceal those exclusions even from local admins and SYSTEM.
Key findings:
- MDAV exclusions can be set four ways: PowerShell (Set-MpPreference or Add-MpPreference), WMI via the MSFT_MpPreference class, Group Policy, or direct registry writes. No matter the method, the result lands in one of two registry locations. PowerShell and WMI-driven exclusions write to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions (written by MsMpEng.exe itself). GPO-driven or direct registry exclusions land at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions, a separate key that MDAV also honors when evaluating what to skip. Path and Extension exclusion types are the most attacker-relevant: they remove a target from real-time protection, scheduled scans, and on-demand scans simultaneously.
- Multiple confirmed campaigns have weaponized this technique. GootKit (2019) set path exclusions via the MSFT_MpPreference WMI class. WhisperGate (2022) excluded the entire C:\ drive using Set-MpPreference. Muddled Libra (2024) also appears in the report as a user of this technique. The tradecraft is not new, but it is persistent and still effective.
- The most forensically significant finding in the Huntress report is the HideExclusionsFromLocalAdmins setting: writing a value to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\HideExclusionsFromLocalAdmins causes Get-MpPreference and similar queries to return no exclusion data, even for local administrators and SYSTEM accounts. The exclusions are still active and still in the registry. They are simply not surfaced through the normal query path. An attacker who sets this after dropping malware into an excluded directory has effectively hidden both the exclusion and the blind spot from standard triage.
- The detection gap matters because many EDR and AV management workflows query exclusions through PowerShell or WMI. If HideExclusionsFromLocalAdmins is set, those queries silently return nothing. The exclusions remain readable by querying the registry directly, specifically the two keys above, but tooling that relies on Get-MpPreference will miss them entirely.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not rely on Get-MpPreference or WMI queries alone to audit Defender exclusions during triage. Read the registry directly. Check both HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions for unexpected paths, and check for the presence of HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\HideExclusionsFromLocalAdmins as a high-confidence indicator of defense evasion in progress. Hunt for reg add or PowerShell Set-MpPreference and Add-MpPreference commands in process creation logs, and correlate the timing of any exclusion write with subsequent file drops into the newly excluded path.

item.title: SC WordPress Malware: A Self-Healing Mesh of Loaders, Drop-Ins, and a Blockchain-Controlled Backdoor
item.description:
SC malware turns WordPress into a self-healing infection mesh, using eight simultaneous persistence points across files, the database, shared memory, and a blockchain-controlled C2 channel that survives every partial cleanup attempt.
Key findings:
- The mesh has eight interlocking components: a .user.ini auto_prepend_file directive pointing at a shim (wp-content/c1b12371.php, name varies), a hidden dot-prefixed string-table loader (.c1b12371.php), two WordPress drop-ins (wp-content/db.php and wp-content/advanced-cache.php), an injected block in the active theme's functions.php, and the backdoor payload installed as both a must-use plugin and a normal plugin (hyper-engine-kit.php in both mu-plugins and plugins, names vary). Each component can independently rebuild all the others, so removing any single piece triggers an immediate rewrite on the next PHP request.
- Three off-disk persistence mechanisms are the reason file-only cleanups fail. The full payload sits in a WordPress options row under a randomized name as a gzip plus base64 blob. A System V shared-memory segment identified by a fixed numeric key holds a PHP copy in RAM that survives both file deletion and database cleanup, and on shared hosting can be owned by a different account. Randomized cron hooks fire on schedule via system cron to redeploy the mesh. Related SC variants also drop database triggers in information_schema.TRIGGERS that recreate an administrator on insert, meaning account deletion is pointless until the trigger is removed.
- The backdoor's C2 uses roughly twenty public Ethereum RPC gateways to read instructions from a smart contract, making domain-based blocking largely ineffective because the whole set of legitimate gateways must be blocked together. Recovered capabilities include checkout skimming via injected front-end JavaScript, remote PHP installation, targeted deactivation and directory-wiping of named security plugins, and cookie-forged authentication for a hidden administrator written directly into the users and usermeta tables, hidden from the admin UI through query and count filters.
- Key IOCs to hunt: unexpected SC_ marker blocks in wp-content/db.php and wp-content/advanced-cache.php, a bounded begin/end block at the bottom of the active theme's functions.php, auto_prepend_file directives in .user.ini, php.ini, or .htaccess pointing at hidden dot-prefixed PHP files, ZIP restore bundles with random hex names in wp-content or uploads, options rows with sc_ prefixed names holding large gzip blobs, and outbound HTTP requests from the web server process to public Ethereum RPC endpoints.
Practitioner takeaway: cleanup order is the operative skill here. First, neutralize the auto_prepend_file by emptying the prepend target to an inert stub before touching the .user.ini directive, because PHP caches that value for up to 300 seconds and deleting the target while the cache is warm kills every PHP request on the account. Second, clear the off-disk copies in this order: remove the payload options row and sc_-prefixed control options from the database, purge the System V shared-memory segment (ipcs and ipcrm on Linux), drop any malicious database triggers found in information_schema.TRIGGERS, and clear the malicious cron hooks. Only after those off-disk sources are gone should you remove files in a single pass. Then delete the hidden administrator and any orphaned options pointing to its ID. A file that returns after this sequence means a persistence point survived. Full IOC list and cleanup guidance are in the Sucuri report.

item.content:encoded:
SC malware turns WordPress into a self-healing infection mesh, using eight simultaneous persistence points across files, the database, shared memory, and a blockchain-controlled C2 channel that survives every partial cleanup attempt.

Key findings:

- The mesh has eight interlocking components: a .user.ini auto_prepend_file directive pointing at a shim (wp-content/c1b12371.php, name varies), a hidden dot-prefixed string-table loader (.c1b12371.php), two WordPress drop-ins (wp-content/db.php and wp-content/advanced-cache.php), an injected block in the active theme's functions.php, and the backdoor payload installed as both a must-use plugin and a normal plugin (hyper-engine-kit.php in both mu-plugins and plugins, names vary). Each component can independently rebuild all the others, so removing any single piece triggers an immediate rewrite on the next PHP request.

- Three off-disk persistence mechanisms are the reason file-only cleanups fail. The full payload sits in a WordPress options row under a randomized name as a gzip plus base64 blob. A System V shared-memory segment identified by a fixed numeric key holds a PHP copy in RAM that survives both file deletion and database cleanup, and on shared hosting can be owned by a different account. Randomized cron hooks fire on schedule via system cron to redeploy the mesh. Related SC variants also drop database triggers in information_schema.TRIGGERS that recreate an administrator on insert, meaning account deletion is pointless until the trigger is removed.

- The backdoor's C2 uses roughly twenty public Ethereum RPC gateways to read instructions from a smart contract, making domain-based blocking largely ineffective because the whole set of legitimate gateways must be blocked together. Recovered capabilities include checkout skimming via injected front-end JavaScript, remote PHP installation, targeted deactivation and directory-wiping of named security plugins, and cookie-forged authentication for a hidden administrator written directly into the users and usermeta tables, hidden from the admin UI through query and count filters.

- Key IOCs to hunt: unexpected SC_ marker blocks in wp-content/db.php and wp-content/advanced-cache.php, a bounded begin/end block at the bottom of the active theme's functions.php, auto_prepend_file directives in .user.ini, php.ini, or .htaccess pointing at hidden dot-prefixed PHP files, ZIP restore bundles with random hex names in wp-content or uploads, options rows with sc_ prefixed names holding large gzip blobs, and outbound HTTP requests from the web server process to public Ethereum RPC endpoints.

First, neutralize the auto_prepend_file by emptying the prepend target to an inert stub before touching the .user.ini directive, because PHP caches that value for up to 300 seconds and deleting the target while the cache is warm kills every PHP request on the account. Only after those off-disk sources are gone should you remove files in a single pass. Then delete the hidden administrator and any orphaned options pointing to its ID. item.title: Russian state hackers use new RedFlick technique to push malware
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 Star Blizzard deploys CosmicPulse backdoor via "RedFlick," a new automated infection chain needing only a single click from the victim, hitting 100+ orgs across the US 🇺🇸, UK 🇬🇧, and Ukraine 🇺🇦 in 2026.
Key details:
- The RedFlick chain starts with a phishing email, then a follow-up containing a password-protected ZIP or RAR. Inside sits a VHDX virtual disk holding an LNK disguised as a PDF. Opening it silently launches a command, shows a decoy PDF, and pulls down an MSI installer, requiring only that one click from the victim rather than the multiple manual steps ClickFix demanded.
- The MSI drops three scheduled tasks with names designed to blend into a legitimate Windows environment: "Internet Quality Test Connection" (beacons hostname and username, can execute a remote DLL), "Network Configuration Manager" (configures WebDAV so remote paths resolve like local ones), and "System Health Monitor" (uses the built-in control.exe to load the next-stage payload). Splitting roles across three tasks is a deliberate evasion move: no single task carries the full chain.
- The next-stage payload is the downloader tracked as NOROBOT and BAITSWITCH, delivered as a Control Panel applet (.cpl). BAITSWITCH fetches two ZIP archives: one holds the Python 3.8 64-bit runtime, the other a bootstrapper script. The bootstrapper reads an encrypted key from the registry, recovers it using an embedded key in AES-ECB mode, then decodes and loads the CosmicPulse backdoor, giving the attacker execution of arbitrary Python code, file download and run, and document exfiltration.
- Targeting since the start of 2026 spans at least 13 distinct large-scale phishing campaigns across 100+ organizations, focused on Ukrainian 🇺🇦 individuals and institutions and international NGOs, think tanks, governments, and financial institutions that have supported Ukraine 🇺🇦 politically or financially. Star Blizzard continues to impersonate trusted contacts using free email providers.
Practitioner takeaway: Three artifacts stand out for hunting. First, look for LNK files inside mounted VHDX images in user download or temp paths: that combination is unusual and worth flagging at the endpoint. Second, audit scheduled tasks created by MSI processes, especially ones invoking control.exe or referencing WebDAV paths in their action fields. Third, hunt registry reads of encrypted blobs followed by Python interpreter execution in the same process tree: that sequence matches the CosmicPulse bootstrapper decryption step. The Microsoft report contains the full technical analysis of the infection chain components.

item.title: Attackers Abuse MSP360 to Deploy ScreenConnect in Dual-RMM Phishing Attacks
item.description:
Unattributed phishing campaign abuses MSP360 RMM as a beachhead to silently deploy ScreenConnect, creating dual remote-access channels that blend into normal IT operations. Microsoft detected the activity in July 2026.
Key details:
- Phishing emails deliver a digitally signed MSP360 RMM v2.5.0.67 installer disguised as meeting invites, Zoom setups, Adobe PDF tools, SSA[.]GOV statements, and e-card RSVPs. File names follow a pattern like ZoomSetup_Installation_v2.5.0.67_oid[redacted].exe. Installers are staged on attacker-controlled infrastructure and legitimate services including Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, GitLab, and Supabase, making network-based blocking harder.
- Once executed, the installer invokes UAC elevation, drops multiple DLLs, and registers two Windows services: RMM.Agent.exe and RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe. It also creates Registry autorun entries to survive reboots and modifies Windows Firewall to permit inbound UDP on port 48678 for RMM.Agent.exe. These are concrete, huntable artifacts.
- MSP360 is then used to run PowerShell that silently installs a ConnectWise ScreenConnect client, giving the attacker a redundant remote-access channel. Post-compromise payloads are executed through ScreenConnect's native RunFile functionality, keeping malicious execution inside a trusted administration workflow and reducing EDR visibility.
- Microsoft also observed a parallel cluster in the same July 2026 timeframe substituting Faronics Deploy Agent for MSP360 before pivoting to ScreenConnect. The common thread is ScreenConnect as the persistent secondary channel, suggesting the actors are rotating initial-access RMM tools to evade detections tied to any single product.
- Scope and attribution: the campaign is unattributed to any known group. The lure variety (government, corporate, software) and use of multiple cloud staging platforms suggest deliberate operational breadth rather than a narrow targeted intrusion.
Hunt for RMM.Agent.exe and RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe as newly registered services, Registry Run keys pointing to MSP360 paths, and Windows Firewall rule changes opening UDP 48678. Cross-reference PowerShell execution under MSP360 parent processes with ScreenConnect installation events. Flag ScreenConnect processes spawning child processes or making outbound connections shortly after MSP360 first-run. Installers arriving from S3, R2, Dropbox, GitLab, or Supabase with RMM version strings in the filename are a strong pre-execution signal worth catching at the email gateway or proxy layer.

item.title: Threat Brief: NetScaler Zero Days CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 Exploited in the Wild (Updated September 30)
item.description:
Two actively exploited NetScaler zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (both CVSS v4.0: 9.5), are delivering web shells across 50,000+ exposed instances as of Sept. 27, 2026.
- CVE-2026-88771 is an unauthenticated RCE via improper input validation on NetScaler ADC and Gateway. CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow in the DTLS configuration that enables RCE or DoS. Both were exploited before Citrix's Sept. 27 disclosure. Earliest observed activity dates to Aug. 21, 2026, with version-fingerprinting requests to /admin_ui/common/css/ns/ui.css and /vpn/js/rdx/core/lang/rdx_en.json.gz hitting more than 100 systems from 104.248.244[.]66 and 77.83.199[.]39.
- Two distinct exploitation chains were observed pre-disclosure. The first uses crafted DTLS traffic to trigger CVE-2026-88772, then drops .deb web shells (e.g., nsgclient18.deb, nsg64.deb) into /vpn/scripts/linux/, a folder normally holding Citrix client packages. The dropped shell nsg64.deb (SHA-256: ae22ef2517b5c0fb47f78745b9cb5260acee0e751b89bcd354640ff8bc8d29ec) is a PHP web shell with RC4-encrypted C2 using key 7489a0f93c67fa5cdaeb4b921d90594d (MD5 of passphrase Rhfajaf1H992), supporting arbitrary command execution, file upload, and chunked file exfiltration. Commands are passed via custom HTTP headers. The shell escalates privileges via the SUID binary at /var/netscaler/.ns_suidcmd.
- The second chain is a three-stage log-poisoning exploit targeting CVE-2026-88771. Stage 1: attacker sends an HTTP request with a Base64-encoded dropper in the User-Agent, which lands in /var/log/httpaccess-vpn.log. Stage 2: a crafted login request injects a shell command after "pitboss PPE missed too many heartbeats NSPPE;" into /var/log/ns.log. Stage 3: the vulnerable Perl script /netscaler/ns_monuploadd_err.pl -WR processes ns.log, extracts the injected text, and pipes it to sh or php. The decoded payload drops .ctxs.receiver into /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/, sets SUID on /bin/sh (chmod 6555), edits /etc/httpd.conf to enable PHP engine and alias the web shell under receiver.min.css, then reloads Apache with kill -HUP. The shell authenticates via a hard-coded CsrfToken cookie value (e826d7ddf3c85920) and executes commands from the NSC_TASS cookie, mimicking legitimate NetScaler session cookie naming.
- Infrastructure used in the pre-disclosure campaign includes 77.83.199[.]39, 78.47.24[.]217, 104.248.244[.]66, 66.135.19[.]18, 167.99.111[.]203, 142.93.85[.]227, 104.248.74[.]206, 137.184.91[.]207, 104.28.247[.]136, 104.28.215[.]136, 104.28.215[.]137, 162.33.178[.]9, 193.149.176[.]207, and 139.180.152[.]138. Actors rotated through Cloudflare WARP VPN addresses and VPS infrastructure, making IP-based blocking insufficient alone. Continuous requests to /logon/LogonPoint/Authentication/GetUserName persisted around the clock through Sept. 27, treat any activity to that path as anomalous.
Patch immediately, but patching does not evict actors already present. For compromise assessment: hunt /vpn/scripts/linux/ for unexpected .deb files, check /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/ for .ctxs.receiver or hidden PHP files, inspect /etc/httpd.conf for injected Alias directives and php_flag engine on modifications, and review /var/log/ns.log for lines containing "pitboss PPE" with text after "NSPPE;". The Unit 42 report includes a detection query for log-poisoning activity targeting ns.log (filter on "pitboss" in citrix_adc_raw), Threat Prevention signature 97562 for CVE-2026-88771, and a full IOC list with hashes and infrastructure. Preserve a VPX snapshot, remote syslog copies, support bundle, and packet engine core dump before patching.

item.title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager flaw exploited
item.description:
CVE-2026-76504 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8, is actively exploited in the wild, and gives unauthenticated remote attackers administrator-level API access to the central management plane of SD-WAN environments.
- CVE-2026-76504 stems from improper handling of URL-encoded characters during request processing against a specific API endpoint. An attacker sends a crafted HTTP request containing URL-encoded variants of the j_security_check authentication path, bypassing the authentication check entirely. No credentials, no user interaction, no foothold elsewhere in the network required. Internet-exposed instances are the primary attack surface, and Cisco confirmed exploitation was occurring before the patch shipped on September 30, 2026.
- The management plane is the target because it is worth more than any single device it manages. Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (formerly Viptela vManage) controls routing policies, network segmentation rules, device configurations, administrative accounts, and site connectivity across every location the SD-WAN environment serves. Unauthorized administrative access here means an adversary can reshape network operations from a single chokepoint rather than pivoting device by device.
- Cisco published two concrete log sources for IR teams. Check /var/log/nms/containers/service-proxy/serviceproxy-access.log for HTTP requests containing encoded variants of the j_security_check path. Check /var/log/nms/vmanage-server.log for authentication events involving usernames that begin with viptela-reserved-. That internal account naming convention is a Viptela legacy carried forward into the Cisco rebrand, and activity against those reserved accounts is a signal the authentication bypass was successfully triggered, not just attempted.
- On-premises deployments require a manual software update. Cisco SD-WAN Cloud (Cisco Managed) customers have already received the fix and need no further action. Remediation version details are accessible through the Help menu in the management interface. While patching is evaluated or deployed, restrict access to the SD-WAN Manager administrative interface to trusted management networks and approved administrative hosts only. Internet exposure with no network-layer control is the condition that makes this trivially exploitable.
Takeaway: Start with exposure. Identify every internet-reachable SD-WAN Manager instance in your environment today. Pull serviceproxy-access.log and search for encoded j_security_check variants. Pull vmanage-server.log and hunt for viptela-reserved- account activity. Any hit on the account pattern should be treated as confirmed compromise and escalated immediately. Correlate suspicious administrative sessions against firewall, proxy, and authentication telemetry because successful exploitation may look like a legitimate admin session once the bypass has fired. The IOCs Cisco published are noted in the report.

item.title: Attackers Exploit Zimbra Flaw to Deploy Web Shells and Harvest Authentication Secrets
item.description:
CVE-2026-73570 in Zimbra Collaboration Suite is actively exploited, CISA KEV-listed, and carries a CVSS score of 8.9. Attackers moved from unauthenticated SMTP to full credential harvest and mailbox exfiltration before the flaw was even publicly disclosed.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated OS command injection flaw triggered by a specially crafted SMTP request when the zimbra-snmp package is installed and SNMP notifications are enabled. No authentication, no user interaction required. Zimbra patched it in version 10.1.20 (July 2026), but Microsoft's telemetry shows active exploitation began July 28, a full two weeks before public disclosure on August 13. CISA added it to KEV with a federal remediation deadline of August 24, 2026.
- The post-exploitation chain is methodical and layered. Attackers ran commands as the "zimbra" service account, dropped JSP web shells into Jetty and mailboxd application paths for redundancy, and used wget or curl to pull additional payloads. Persistence was established through cron, systemd (a service named "zimlog.service"), memfd_create for memory-backed execution, SSH authorized_keys additions, and local account creation. Privilege escalation came via modification of /etc/pam.d/sudo to grant the zimbra account unrestricted passwordless sudo.
- Rather than targeting individual mailbox passwords, attackers used "zmlocalconfig -s" to extract Zimbra's centralized authentication secrets directly, recovering zimbraPreAuthKey, zimbraAuthTokenKey, and zimbraTwoFactorAuthSecret. A Go-based implant then parsed /opt/zimbra/conf/localconfig.xml to build MySQL and LDAP connection strings and export the mailbox, mailbox_metadata, and mobile_devices tables, plus the full zimbra.* namespace. Harvested data was compressed into a ZIP and staged for exfiltration.
- In at least one campaign, a lightweight shell downloader retrieved a "Zimdown2" Go binary that installed the "Zimclient2" remote-access agent, supporting interactive shell, bidirectional file transfer, and SOCKS5 proxying over WebSocket, TLS, or raw TCP. Lateral movement across cluster nodes used Zimbra's own SSH identity at /opt/zimbra/.ssh/zimbra_identity with rsync to distribute web shells.
- In one confirmed case, the attacker staged mailbox backup content as /opt/zimbra/final.tar.gz and attempted exfiltration via AzCopy (downloaded from hxxps://aka[.]ms/downloadazcopy-v10-linux) to wsweb03.blob.core[.]windows[.]net/log/windows.log using an operator-supplied Azure Blob SAS URL. Whether the transfer completed is unconfirmed.
Practitioner takeaway: If you run Zimbra, patch to 10.1.20 immediately or uninstall zimbra-snmp and restrict SNMP/SMTP to trusted hosts as interim mitigation. For response and hunting, CERT Polska flagged /var/log/zimbra.log for suspicious service restarts as the first triage step. Then sweep Jetty and mailboxd webapps directories and /tmp for JSP web shells created after July 20. Check /etc/pam.d/sudo for unauthorized modifications, review /etc/systemd/system/ for zimlog.service or any unfamiliar unit files, and audit /opt/zimbra/.ssh/authorized_keys and local account additions. Run "zmlocalconfig -s" output against your expected secrets baseline and rotate zimbraPreAuthKey, zimbraAuthTokenKey, and zimbraTwoFactorAuthSecret if compromise is suspected. Hunt process trees for zmprov, zmlocalconfig, rsync, AzCopy, and memfd_create-backed processes spawned from the zimbra account. The full IOC list and attack-chain detail are in Microsoft's report.

item.title: TerminalFix and Lorem Ipsum Loader enable covert tunneling
item.description:
STAC4924 campaign links TerminalFix lures and Lorem Ipsum Loader to GOLD VICTOR, deploying a Python WebSocket tunnel active since at least March 2026 across two distinct delivery phases.
Key findings:
- TerminalFix is a ClickFix variant that directs victims to open a Windows Terminal window rather than the Run dialog, executing a PowerShell command that downloads a ZIP containing a legitimate binary, malicious DLL, and batch script. The batch script installs persistence and launches a legitimate executable (lockscreencontentserver.exe) that sideloads dui70.dll, which contains and runs Lorem Ipsum Loader. That loader evades entropy-based detection by encoding shellcode bytes as plain English words mapped to hex values via a lookup table.
- Lorem Ipsum Loader uses letsdiskuss[.]com as a dead-drop resolver: it fetches an attacker-controlled profile from that platform to retrieve the current C2 server list, then communicates with C2 via HTTP POST requests disguised as JPEG image files containing steganographically encoded data. A portable Python runtime is dropped to Users\Public\indigo, and client[.]py establishes an encrypted WebSocket reverse tunnel, assigning each compromised host a unique UUID.
- The campaign ran two phases: March-April used SEO-poisoned sites serving trojanized Microsoft Teams MSI installers signed with fraudulently obtained certificates. In late May, after Microsoft disrupted the malware-signing service supplying those certificates, the campaign pivoted to TerminalFix lures. DLL sideloading introduced in Phase 1 became the execution core of Phase 2, with 19 documented sideload pairings spanning pairs like changepk.exe/slc.dll, werfault secure.exe/faultrep.dll, and wuauclt.exe/sspicli.dll.
- Persistence across both phases uses auto-run registry entries masquerading as Microsoft or software-update components, often reinforced with scheduled tasks. The per-victim UUID callback structure and letsdiskuss[.]com dead-drop resolver appear across both phases, and Sophos attributes STAC4924 with moderate confidence to GOLD VICTOR (also tracked as Vanilla Tempest, Rapid Brigantine, VICE SPIDER, and linked to Vice Society and Rhysida ransomware), though no ransomware encryption has been observed in this campaign yet.
Takeaway: Hunt for Python runtime deployments under Users\Public\indigo, outbound WebSocket connections from python.exe, and unsigned DLLs loaded by the sideload pairs listed above. Check auto-run registry entries and scheduled tasks impersonating Microsoft or update services. Inspect HTTP traffic for JPEG-wrapped POST bodies and DNS or HTTP calls to letsdiskuss[.]com. Sophos detection rules Evade_28d, C2_38a, Evade_61b, Creds_2d, Troj/Loader-RV, Troj/Loader-RW, Troj/Loader-RT, and ATK/PyTune-B cover this threat. Full IOC list is in the SophosLabs GitHub repository.

item.title: Stolen GitHub Token (PAT): Incident Response Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Compromised GitHub PATs are fueling a wave of source-code exfiltration incidents in 2026, with one stolen token routinely snowballing into 1,100+ exposed secrets across AWS, Azure, GCP, and CI/CD pipelines.
Key findings:
- The attack chain is consistent across cases Invictus IR has worked this year: token stolen from a developer endpoint via infostealer or malicious browser extension, automated API reconnaissance against /repositories/{id}/readme endpoints generating thousands of api.request events in minutes, bulk repository cloning, then secret harvesting that pivots into cloud platforms, SaaS, and internal systems. Developer workstations are the primary target because one compromised machine can yield source code, stored credentials, and development tooling simultaneously.
- Classic PATs (prefix ghp_) dominate these cases and carry the worst blast radius: they inherit the compromised identity's full repository access and may never expire. Fine-grained PATs (github_pat_) limit exposure to named repositories and permissions. A stolen GitHub App private key is the worst case of all because it mints fresh installation tokens on demand across every App installation until the key itself is rotated. Revoking a token against an App key compromise does nothing.
- GitHub telemetry gaps are the investigation's biggest enemy. git.clone and git.fetch events are retained for only 7 days and are accessible via REST API only, never in the web UI. api.request events (the ones that reveal the enumeration sweep) are available exclusively through audit log streaming, which must be explicitly enabled before the incident. Organizations on Free or Team plans get neither. If streaming was not configured in advance, the clone record is almost certainly gone by the time responders arrive.
- Scoping rule from the report: where telemetry exists, scope to what it proves. Where it does not, the blast radius is the ceiling, not zero. A missing git.clone is evidence of absent logging, not an untouched repository. In one documented case, a single compromised token led to 300+ repositories cloned and more than 1,100 potential secrets identified across AWS, Azure, GCP, GitHub, Slack, and Snowflake. Validating and rotating those secrets required 30+ people across security, IT, and engineering for over a week.
- Initial access investigation must move off GitHub entirely. GitHub shows post-use activity only. Hunt the affected endpoint in EDR telemetry for infostealer execution, suspicious credential store or browser access, unusual archive creation, and processes touching Git config files or CLI authentication state. Also check whether the token was exposed in public repositories or Git history using secret scanning or tools like TruffleHog, and review GitHub secret scanning alerts to see if the token was flagged before the compromise.
Practitioner takeaway: Before anything else, identify the token prefix to set your blast radius ceiling, then pull Git events via the Audit Log REST API immediately because the 7-day window is already counting down. Check whether audit log streaming was enabled and whether api.request events were captured: thousands of readme endpoint hits in a short window is your enumeration signal. For every repository in scope, treat the full contents and full Git history as exfiltrated and start the secret validity triage from there. For hardening, the report recommends migrating broadly scoped classic PATs to fine-grained tokens or GitHub Apps, and replacing stored cloud credentials in workflows with OIDC entirely. Full guidance including token type reference tables and blast radius scoping methodology is in the report.

item.title: ShinyHunters Claims FBIJobs.gov Breach: New Zero-Day, CVE-2026-35273 Bypass, or Third-Party Failure?
item.description:
ShinyHunters claims breach of FBIJobs[.]gov, exfiltrating up to 3 TB of FBI employee PII. CVE-2026-35273 WAF bypass is the leading initial access hypothesis, with both portals still offline a week later.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-35273 is a critical (CVSS 9.8) unauthenticated RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft's Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), triggered via Java deserialization. ShinyHunters exploited it as a zero-day May 27 to June 9, 2026, before Oracle's June 10 out-of-band patch. The new wrinkle documented September 25: the group modified its exploit to hit /%50SEMHUB/ instead of /PSEMHUB/. %50 is URL-encoded "P". WAF rules matching the literal string before normalization miss it entirely; WebLogic decodes and routes it to the vulnerable servlet. Organizations that blocked the path but never patched were re-exposed.
- Post-exploitation tooling documented in the September 25 Mandiant report includes two JSP web shells (x.jsp for command execution, u.jsp for chunked uploads), a trojanized installer Ple64.exe loading a backdoor tracked as SIDEEYE (SHA-256: 3ba215692665513abfffd4e815c5c45f2d41e5dcc4283a2a3b740930c5c417c3), Neo-reGeorg tunnels (tunnel.jsp, tunnel.jspx) for SOCKS proxying, and MeshAgent for persistent remote access via winmanage-me[.]network and azurenetfiles[.]net. The report also notes fileless command execution leaving no JSP on disk, meaning file-based detections alone are insufficient.
- What is confirmed vs. claimed: the FBI confirmed unauthorized activity and an active investigation. A 5,000-record sample shared with journalists was judged authentic by 404 Media and Reuters, containing names, home addresses, spouse details, Social Security numbers, unit assignments, and psychiatric and medical files. The 2 to 3 TB total, access to MedLink, Criminal Justice, BEAST, BICS, and FBI-managed AWS GovCloud are actor claims only. An internal FBI memo reported by The New York Times says the Bureau is operating under the assumption that personal data of all employees was exfiltrated, framed as a protective planning posture, not confirmation of system-level claims.
- The data combination is the real threat: identity plus home address plus spouse details plus unit assignment plus medical records creates a physical targeting and foreign intelligence mapping risk. If the MedLink and Criminal Justice access claims hold, it points to a catastrophic segmentation failure: a public-facing recruitment portal with a path to medical and investigative systems, whether through the FBI's own environment or a third-party host the FBI has not yet ruled out.
- Attribution carries noise: the defacement used ASCII Umbreon art tied to Dutch 🇳🇱 suspect Pepijn van der Stap, arrested September 16, but the imagery predates his use of the alias and may be deliberate misdirection by ShinyHunters' current leadership. A Rotterdam court ordered him held 90 days on September 29. No authority has publicly linked him to FBIJobs[.]gov. ShinyHunters is a brand with competing factions, not a fixed crew. Handle, artwork, and leak-site branding are weak attribution signals on their own.
Hunt now in WebLogic access logs for POST bursts of 5 to 15 requests to /hub from external IPs, and grep for /%50SEMHUB/ and any percent-encoded variants alongside the literal path. Check every WebLogic node for x.jsp, u.jsp, tunnel.jsp, tunnel.jspx, and Ple64.exe in PSEMHUB.war and PORTAL.war. Alert on cmd.exe or bash spawned by the WebLogic Java process. Hunt for MeshCentral agents and for zstd, rsync, sshpass, or curl running under PeopleSoft service accounts. Key IOCs: SIDEEYE C2 at 162.219.30[.]165 (TCP 3333/3334), exfil staging at 104.219.234[.]138, scanner at 5.199.162[.]157. If you find a shell, rotate all credentials readable by the PeopleSoft service account immediately: psappsrv.cfg connection strings, Integration Broker credentials, and any cloud keys reachable from the web tier. Full IOC list and hashes are in the report.

item.title: Attackers Abuse ChatGPT Custom GPTs to Deliver RAT via ClickFix Lures
item.description:
ChatGPT Custom GPTs weaponized as ClickFix lure delivery points, dropping a fully featured RAT via DLL sideloading and WAV-embedded payloads. At least 40 confirmed infections observed by Huntress in late September 2026.
Key findings:
- Attackers created two Custom GPTs named "Plus 5.6" and promoted them via Google sponsored search results. The malicious GPT links are chatgpt[.]com/g/g-6ab595ad6554819181b686d4876efb80-plus-5-6 and chatgpt[.]com/g/g-6ab6ba039440819185ed491740b11cf8-plus-5-6. When a user interacts with either, the GPT responds with a Google Sites link presenting a fake "Service Availability Notice," directing victims to a backup domain for immediate access. That domain presents a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA that triggers a ClickFix PowerShell execution lure.
- The PowerShell command deploys an MSI installer named ISOSimple.msi, which abuses a legitimate Canon-signed binary, COTFileReadApp.exe, to sideload a rogue DLL named ceiinfolog.dll. That DLL is an altered Canon binary that loads a second unsigned DLL, rdCore.dll, which extracts an encrypted loader from a WAV audio file named Common.Integrator.Preview.wav. The final loader unpacks the trojan and a persistence script from an encrypted file named monitor.raw, placing this technique in the same family as Octowave Loader campaigns previously known to hide payloads in audio formats.
- Before executing, the loader bypasses AMSI, unhooks ntdll.dll to sidestep user-mode monitoring, and runs anti-VM checks against CPU vendor strings for VMware, VirtualBox, Hyper-V, QEMU, Xen, and Parallels drivers and services. The RAT then resolves its C2, referred to internally as the "Gate," using DNS-over-HTTPS through Cloudflare, Google, and Quad9 resolvers, meaning C2 lookups travel inside ordinary HTTPS traffic and never appear in local DNS logs.
- The RAT is fully featured: it profiles installed antivirus and Microsoft Defender status, runs remote desktop and screen broadcast sessions, captures camera, microphone, and system audio, recognizes 17 web browsers, includes a file manager, and drops secondary payloads including EXE, DLL, MSI, PowerShell, batch, VBScript, and JavaScript. It consistently drops a legitimately signed binary named GOMCam2024.exe, which launches Google Chrome with a throwaway browser profile under the %TEMP% directory.
- This campaign is part of a broader ClickFix surge covered in the Huntress report: separate campaigns are abusing Google Sites impersonating OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude to deliver in-memory stealers, EtherHiding via compromised sites to drop Amatera Stealer (linked to Russian-aligned cluster UAT-10820 targeting Ukrainian 🇺🇦 government systems), and a campaign active since at least November 2025 using 31 compromised business websites and Polygon blockchain-based C2 resolution.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for COTFileReadApp.exe and GOMCam2024.exe appearing outside their expected Canon or GOM software install paths, and look for child processes spawned from msiexec.exe loading unsigned DLLs alongside legitimate signed ones. Check for Chrome launched by GOMCam2024.exe with a profile path resolving into %TEMP%. Because the RAT uses DNS-over-HTTPS, standard DNS telemetry will be blind to C2 resolution; look for high-frequency HTTPS connections to known DoH resolver IPs (Cloudflare 1.1.1[.]1, Google 8.8.8[.]8, Quad9 9.9.9[.]9) from unexpected processes. WAV and RAW files in software installation directories warrant examination for embedded encrypted content. The full IOC list is in the Huntress report.

That domain presents a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA that triggers a ClickFix PowerShell execution lure.

- The PowerShell command deploys an MSI installer named ISOSimple.msi, which abuses a legitimate Canon-signed binary, COTFileReadApp.exe, to sideload a rogue DLL named ceiinfolog.dll. That DLL is an altered Canon binary that loads a second unsigned DLL, rdCore.dll, which extracts an encrypted loader from a WAV audio file named Common.Integrator.Preview.wav. The final loader unpacks the trojan and a persistence script from an encrypted file named monitor.raw, placing this technique in the same family as Octowave Loader campaigns previously known to hide payloads in audio formats.

- Before executing, the loader bypasses AMSI, unhooks ntdll.dll to sidestep user-mode monitoring, and runs anti-VM checks against CPU vendor strings for VMware, VirtualBox, Hyper-V, QEMU, Xen, and Parallels drivers and services. The RAT then resolves its C2, referred to internally as the "Gate," using DNS-over-HTTPS through Cloudflare, Google, and Quad9 resolvers, meaning C2 lookups travel inside ordinary HTTPS traffic and never appear in local DNS logs.

- The RAT is fully featured: it profiles installed antivirus and Microsoft Defender status, runs remote desktop and screen broadcast sessions, captures camera, microphone, and system audio, recognizes 17 web browsers, includes a file manager, and drops secondary payloads including EXE, DLL, MSI, PowerShell, batch, VBScript, and JavaScript. It consistently drops a legitimately signed binary named GOMCam2024.exe, which launches Google Chrome with a throwaway browser profile under the %TEMP% directory.

- This campaign is part of a broader ClickFix surge covered in the Huntress report: separate campaigns are abusing Google Sites impersonating OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude to deliver in-memory stealers, EtherHiding via compromised sites to drop Amatera Stealer (linked to Russian-aligned cluster UAT-10820 targeting Ukrainian 🇺🇦 government systems), and a campaign active since at least November 2025 using 31 compromised business websites and Polygon blockchain-based C2 resolution.

Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for COTFileReadApp.exe and GOMCam2024.exe appearing outside their expected Canon or GOM software install paths, and look for child processes spawned from msiexec.exe loading unsigned DLLs alongside legitimate signed ones. Check for Chrome launched by GOMCam2024.exe with a profile path resolving into %TEMP%. Because the RAT uses DNS-over-HTTPS, standard DNS telemetry will be blind to C2 resolution; look for high-frequency HTTPS connections to known DoH resolver IPs (Cloudflare 1.1.1[.]1, Google 8.8.8[.]8, Quad9 9.9.9[.]9) from unexpected processes. WAV and RAW files in software installation directories warrant examination for embedded encrypted content. The full IOC list is in the Huntress report.

item.title: 2CLoader: A New Malware Loader Delivering Vidar and Remus
item.description:
2CLoader, a new loader first observed in August 2026, delivers Vidar and Remus info-stealers via a heavily configurable PE-resource payload system with layered decryption, indirect syscalls, and runtime environment spoofing.
Key findings:
- The loader stores its encrypted payload and config in a PE resource, with the last 0xDC bytes forming the config structure identified by the magic bytes 2C 3D 4E 5F. Decryption is a three-stage process: rolling XOR using rolling_xor_seed, a second XOR pass with xor_key_after_rolling_xor, and finally AES-GCM using a key derived from the SHA256 of the loader's own .text section. That self-referential key derivation means a dumped or modified sample produces a wrong key automatically. An anti-emulation timing trap XORs all 32 digest bytes with 0xFF if a 3,000,000-iteration arithmetic loop completes in under 2,000,000 CPU cycles, silently invalidating the key for sandboxes. ThreatLabz has published a Python payload decryption script to their GitHub.
- 2CLoader uses Hell's Gate to perform indirect system calls against NtProtectVirtualMemory, NtUnmapViewOfSection, NtQueryInformationProcess, NtDelayExecution, NtSetContextThread, and NtGetContextThread, mapping a clean ntdll from disk and scanning for the syscall gadget 0F 05 C3 (syscall, ret). If initialization fails, it falls back to GetProcAddress. On top of that, if opt_flag bit 0x400 is set, the loader patches roughly 20 Windows APIs with inline trampoline hooks to spoof system identity: GetUserNameA/W returns one of (admin, user, gamer, john, alex, player), GetComputerNameA/W returns a DESKTOP- prefixed random name, GetVolumeInformationA/W randomizes the volume serial, and RegQueryValueExA/W swaps BaseBoardManufacturer and MachineGuid with plausible-looking fake values. InternetReadFile and WinHttpReadData replace the last two octets of any IPv4 addresses in received network data with random values, likely to corrupt C2 address extraction by analysts or sandboxes.
- Persistence is controlled by the persistence_option bitmask and can combine six methods simultaneously: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (value name SecurityHealthService.exe), HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce (same name), Startup folder copy, a scheduled task via XML with a LogonTrigger named SecurityHealthService.exe, HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows Load value, and HKCU\Environment UserInitMprLogonScript. Payload injection defaults to a suspended dllhost.exe (RunPE) or an in-process manual PE load (LoadPE); the RunPE path uses NtSetInformationFile FileDispositionInformation to mark a temp file DeletePending before creating an image section from it with NtCreateSection SEC_IMAGE, a technique that leaves no persistent dropped file. If opt_flag 0x80 is set, the optional secondary payload is spawned with PPID spoofed to explorer.exe.
- C2 communication uses HTTP POST to /api/beacon with a Chrome-spoofed User-Agent. The POST body is a JSON registration blob XOR-encrypted with the static 32-byte key (4A 7B 3C 1D 8E 5F A0 D1 62 93 24 F5 B6 47 C8 09 E1 72 53 84 35 A6 D7 18 49 FA 0B 6C 9D 2E BF 50). The registration message includes the malware config ID, OS build, PID, privilege level, locale, payload execution flags, and the pn field which contains a filename such as default.exe or build_tbuild.exe, useful for build tracking. The confirmed C2 is hxxps://aware-cr1[.]com/api/beacon and a delivery URL observed in the wild is hxxp://62.60.226[.]185/t0907.exe.
- Anti-VM scoring uses a hybrid model: hard-fail on CPUID hypervisor vendor (VMware, VirtualBox, KVM, Xen, Parallels, QEMU TCG blocked; Hyper-V allowed), matching module names, process names, MAC prefixes, and registry keys tied to VirtualBox, VMware, and Wine. If those pass, a score-based check requires 8 of 11 environmental conditions including process count above 25, at least 2 GB RAM, 40 GB disk, screen resolution larger than 800x600, at least 2 recent files in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent, and cursor movement within 500 ms. A single anti-VM pass taking over 200 ms also triggers failure.
Hunt focus: look for scheduled tasks and Run keys named SecurityHealthService.exe owned by non-SYSTEM accounts, dllhost.exe or svchost.exe processes with a command line spoofed to svchost.exe and no legitimate parent, and outbound HTTP POST to /api/beacon with Content-Type application/octet-stream. For memory forensics, scan for the config magic 2C 3D 4E 5F in process memory and look for the syscall gadget scan pattern in ntdll-mapped regions. ThreatLabz provides 19 SHA256 hashes, defanged IOCs, and a payload decryption script in the report, with the full anti-VM blocklist on their GitHub.

item.title: Unauthenticated command injection on internet-facing mail servers: tracking CVE-2026-73570
item.description:
CVE-2026-73570: Unauthenticated OS command injection in Zimbra Collaboration Suite's SNMP notification path is actively exploited in the wild, listed in CISA KEV, and delivers full mail-store access, credential theft, and persistent remote-access implants.
Key findings:
- The vulnerability lives in the swatchdog-to-snmptrap execution path. A crafted SMTP request injects shell metacharacters into SNMP notification processing, executing as the zimbra service account with no authentication required. Exploitation requires the optional zimbra-snmp package installed and SNMP notifications enabled. Patch to Zimbra 10.1.20 (released July 20, 2026) immediately. If patching must wait, uninstall zimbra-snmp, disable SNMP notifications, and restrict SMTP and SNMP access to trusted hosts only. Microsoft telemetry captured active exploitation between the patch release and public disclosure on August 13, 2026, meaning attackers operated with knowledge of the vulnerability before defenders had a CVE to work from. The MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed span T1595.002, T1190, T1059.004, T1105, T1068, T1053.003, T1543.002, T1505.003, T1036.005, T1620, T1083, T1071.001, T1102.001, T1560.001, T1074.001, and T1496.
- The post-exploitation chain is deep and deliberate. After initial access, attackers deployed multiple JSP webshells into Jetty and mailboxd application paths and propagated them via the existing zimbra SSH identity at /opt/zimbra/.ssh/zimbra_identity and rsync to peer mailbox nodes. Privilege escalation abused the interaction between zmmailboxdmgr, its writable log directory, pam_exec, and zmstat-fd to make /etc/pam.d/sudo writable by the zimbra account, then added a NOPASSWD: ALL sudoers entry. The sudoers file was written to /etc/sudoers.d/81_metric. A persistence service named zimlog.service was dropped into /etc/systemd/system/ and timestomped to match the modification times of rsync.service and sshd.service. Memory-backed execution used memfd_create via /proc/self/fd. C2 included an OpenSSL reverse shell over a named pipe at /tmp/s and a zimclient2 WebSocket agent at psk1zim.abrdns[.]com/agentws with TLS and raw TCP fallbacks. One campaign stage polled encrypted commands from a Base blockchain contract at 0x25bdA7Feb3553995AD68a9A8Ed8c731b73a71586 over public JSON-RPC.
- Credential and mailbox collection was purpose-built. A Go binary with embedded module path zimbra-exfil/client-dump reads /opt/zimbra/conf/localconfig.xml and extracts mysql_root_password, zimbra_mysql_password, ldap_root_password, and six additional LDAP service credentials, then exports full contents from the mailbox, mailbox_metadata, mobile_devices, and out_of_office tables plus all zimbra.* namespace tables. A separate dumpSecrets function retrieves zimbraAuthTokenKey from cn=config,cn=zimbra, which enables forging valid session tokens for any account without credentials, and zimbraPreAuthKey, which enables pre-authenticated login URL construction for any user. Collected material was staged under /tmp/zimbra_dump_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS/ and compressed. On one host, mail-store backup content was archived to /opt/zimbra/final.tar.gz and an AzCopy transfer was attempted to wsweb03.blob.core[.]windows[.]net/log/windows.log using an operator-supplied SAS URL. Transfer completion was not confirmed.
- The pre-disclosure reconnaissance window is a critical hunting interval. Between July 28 and August 7, two distinct scanning tools probed the injection path using the ZB73570 User-Agent and out-of-band callbacks to oast[.]fun, oast[.]online, dnslog.pp[.]ua, requestrepo[.]com, and bypass[.]eu[.]org subdomains. This activity predates the 30-day Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting retention window as of today. Defenders must search Sentinel or archived logs for the second-stage infrastructure. Key C2 IPs include 45.32.30[.]235:8081 and 8080, 193.42.40[.]135:443, and 3.209.137[.]175:443. Dropper domains include transzimbra.linkpc[.]net and wslogzimbra.linkpc[.]net. The S3-hosted dropper URL was mexico-cashpay-test.s3.dualstack.mx-central-1.amazonaws[.]com/pakistan/2026/aliyun_update.tar.gz. Key SHA-256 hashes include zimclient2 at b594a42b8f1c6f090327bb9a3361c2d3515537fb7ac8da6b9061b9a3f330e159 and zimdown2 at bf28f38122bf20d5fac969cc414daa6a890cdea872d389ca93d2092b6b7773cf.
Practitioner takeaway: On any confirmed Zimbra host, do not stop at quarantining a named payload. Several of the most consequential outcomes involved only a plain shell. Hunt for perl spawning sh or bash via a .swatchdog_script command line containing snmptrap and shell metacharacters. Check every mailbox node for unexpected JSP files and generated _jsp.java artifacts in jetty_base/webapps/, mailboxd/webapps/, and work/zimbra/jsp/. Inspect /etc/systemd/system/ for units with zimbra or logging names, unusual ownership, or timestamps matching sshd.service or rsync.service. Rotate zimbraPreAuthKey and zimbraAuthTokenKey immediately: possession of either value enables account takeover without credentials. Seven Microsoft Defender XDR Advanced Hunting queries covering the full attack chain, the full IOC list, and all named Defender detections are in the report.

item.title: Beware of Malware infection in Facebook Ads Offering Cryptocurrency Rewards
item.description:
JSCEAL, a Node.js-based infostealer, is spreading through Facebook-targeted ads impersonating cryptocurrency exchanges, with roughly 1,500 confirmed infections across Windows and macOS systems in Korea over August-September 2026.
- The attack chain opens on Facebook with ads promising cryptocurrency rewards for installing an "official" exchange app. Clicking redirects to a convincing fake exchange site that mirrors the real brand's logo, color scheme, and live price feeds. Behind that facade, embedded malicious JavaScript fingerprints the visitor's OS, pulls configuration from an attacker-controlled server, and dynamically generates a platform-specific installer: a BAT file for Windows, a PKG file for macOS. The user never sees the generation happen.
- On Windows, the BAT file is the first stage loader. It invokes PowerShell to pull additional code from an external server, tampers with Microsoft Defender by adding scan exclusions to suppress detection, registers a scheduled task for persistence, and drops a desktop shortcut at Users\Public\Desktop\Binance.LNK to sell the illusion of a legitimate install. The scheduled task is the persistence anchor and the mechanism that communicates with the C2 for follow-on commands. A compressed archive is then downloaded, decompressed, and the embedded Node.js runtime executes the JSCEAL payload as JavaScript or compiled V8 bytecode.
- On macOS, the PKG postinstall script downloads and runs a secondary shell script, deletes temporary files to reduce traces, then presents a language-matched dialog box prompting the user for their account password. The script actively verifies the entered password against actual account credentials and writes it to a separate file. It also exfiltrates the Machine ID, computer name, clipboard contents, and PKG filename to an external server before registering a LaunchAgent for persistence and staging the Node.js environment for JSCEAL payload execution.
- DFIR artifact focus for Windows: PowerShell execution history, Microsoft Defender exclusion registry modifications, scheduled task XML definitions (Task Scheduler operational log at Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler%4Operational.evtx), and the Binance.LNK shortcut under Users\Public\Desktop. For macOS: LaunchAgent plist files in /Library/LaunchAgents or ~/Library/LaunchAgents, shell script execution traces, any file created by the postinstall script holding a captured password, and outbound connections made during the PKG installation window. Clipboard data exfiltration means memory forensics or clipboard history artifacts may also hold investigative value.
Practitioners responding to a suspected JSCEAL infection should prioritize pulling scheduled task definitions and Defender exclusion logs on Windows, and LaunchAgent entries alongside any password-capture files on macOS. Hunt for Node.js processes spawning JavaScript or V8 bytecode that arrived as a downloaded archive, and look for PowerShell reaching out to external hosts shortly after a BAT execution. The AhnLab ASEC report contains the full IOC list; pull it before scoping.

item.title: Attackers Exploit NetScaler Flaw for Root Access, Deploy WHIPSHOT and SLAPSHOT
item.description:
CVE-2026-88772 (CVSS 9.5) pre-auth root exploit in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway is under active mass exploitation, with dozens of organizations hit across government, finance, tech, education, and legal sectors in North America and Europe.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88772 is a heap memory overflow in the DTLS protocol handling within the NetScaler Packet Processing Engine (NSPPE), running on the underlying FreeBSD platform. Sending malformed or fragmented DTLS record headers during the pre-auth handshake corrupts heap boundaries and diverts control flow to execute arbitrary shellcode as root. No authentication required. CVE-2026-88771 is a companion flaw being exploited in parallel, with CERT-EU observing attackers filling HTTP logs with Base64-encoded payloads in the User-Agent string and hammering authentication logs in timing-sensitive trigger sequences.
- The post-exploitation chain begins by modifying httpd.conf to treat .deb files as PHP scripts, enabling web shell staging. A covert second-stage config maps incoming requests to .ico files under /vpn/media/ to corresponding .sig files in /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/scripts/linux/, effectively disguising PHP web shell execution as image requests. Permissions on /bin/sh are then modified before a full appliance reboot to entrench persistence through the reboot cycle.
- WHIPSHOT is the primary PHP web shell, extracting Base64-encoded commands and payloads from native HTTP headers, executing them, and returning results, making it blend with normal traffic at the header level. SLAPSHOT is a Python TCP tunneler that bridges WHIPSHOT to internal network hosts for reconnaissance, lateral movement, and credential harvesting. If no command or session is received within 10 minutes, SLAPSHOT removes its port and lock files and terminates itself to reduce forensic footprint.
- Detection is non-trivial but the artifacts are specific. Look for unauthorized modifications to httpd.conf and httperror-vpn logs showing missing .sig file errors, indicating attackers probing for shells across multiple environments. Web server access logs may show GET requests returning HTTP 404 with elevated processing durations and multi-kilobyte response sizes, a key anomaly given the 404 status. Examine /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/scripts/linux/ for unexpected .sig and .deb files, and check /vpn/media/ request paths mapping to non-image file execution.
- Scope is significant. Censys counted 42,735 NetScaler hosts as of September 28, 2026, with the United States 🇺🇸 accounting for 32% of exposed hosts. GreyNoise observed mass reconnaissance beginning September 28 that escalated into full mass exploitation the same evening, now spanning multiple independent threat actors pursuing botnet recruitment and access brokering, well beyond the initial targeted intrusions Mandiant documented.
Hunt priority: query web server access logs for .ico requests under /vpn/media/ returning 404 with response sizes above a few kilobytes, and pull httperror-vpn logs for .sig missing-file errors. Audit httpd.conf for mod_php enablement and .deb or .sig handler entries you did not configure. Because these appliances sit outside EDR visibility, log review and file integrity checks on the paths above are your primary forensic surface. Patch immediately and treat any unpatched NetScaler exposed to the internet as potentially implanted.

item.title: Attackers Abuse ChatGPT Custom GPTs to Deploy a Full-Featured RAT
item.description:
ChatGPT Custom GPTs abused as a RAT delivery surface: attackers built a fake "Plus 5.6" GPT on the real chatgpt[.]com domain, chaining ClickFix, DLL sideloading, and a custom encrypted archive to deploy a full-featured RAT across at least 40 confirmed incidents.
- The entry point is a sponsored Google search result landing on a legitimate chatgpt[.]com Custom GPT page. Any interaction triggers a redirect to a Google Sites page serving a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA. The ClickFix prompt instructs the victim to paste a PowerShell one-liner into Windows Run. That command uses a decimal-encoded IP address to evade URL filters, downloads a 27,000-character script composed of negative numbers, decodes it entirely in memory, and installs ISOSimple.msi, which masquerades as an "Advanced Printer Configuration Reader" from a publisher called Softplicity and hides itself from the installed programs list. Microsoft Defender quarantined the MSI in at least one case, but by then dual persistence (a Run key and a scheduled task) had already landed.
- The technical core is DLL sideloading through COTFileReadApp.exe, a legitimately signed Canon binary from the CaptureOnTouch product. Attackers replaced its companion logging library COTFileReadApp.dll with a near-identical version that exports the same functions Canon expects but adds one extra import: rdCore.dll, where the malicious code lives. Windows loads whatever sits next to the EXE with the right name, so the signed Canon binary does the work. A second wave swapped Canon for a Stardock-signed binary, same loader and RAT, different signed application and filenames, proving the signed-binary layer is interchangeable.
- Payload delivery hides inside media files and custom archives. rdCore.dll extracts an encrypted loader from a bundled WAV file: the file has a valid audio header and real audio data at the start, but the actual sound data stops midway and encrypted payload bytes follow. The WAV header claims roughly 700KB, the file is over 1MB. A rolling XOR cipher decodes the loader in memory. The loader then finds monitor.raw, a homemade encrypted archive containing 315 folders, 806 files, a persistence script, and the RAT. Each file carries its own encryption key, the index uses per-entry salts, and a master key embedded in the loader is required to read any of it. The Stardock variant hid the loader inside a genuine Microsoft NuGet package instead of the WAV file, and its delivery script strips the Mark-of-the-Web tag from the MSI before execution, bypassing SmartScreen entirely.
- The RAT is full-featured: remote desktop, screen and camera and audio capture, credential harvesting from 17 browsers, file search, and arbitrary payload execution in nine formats. C2 resolution uses DNS-over-HTTPS via Cloudflare, Google, and Quad9, keeping DNS queries inside HTTPS traffic and out of local DNS logs. OpenAI pulled the first reported Custom GPT on September 25; a replacement tied to the same campaign was live two days later.
Huntress's detection framing is the right anchor here: hunt the behavior chain, not the signed binary names. Look for PowerShell spawning msiexec against a GUID-named MSI in the temp folder, a Canon or Stardock binary (or any signed binary) executing from an unexpected path under AppData, and a Run key or scheduled task that resurrects after removal. For the C2 angle, monitor for DoH queries to Cloudflare or Google resolver endpoints from processes that have no business making them. The PowerShell-to-msiexec-to-signed-app-sideload-to-persistence sequence has held across every variant; detections tied to specific binary names will miss the next swap. Full IOC list and technical details are in the Huntress report.

item.title: China-nexus UAT-11587 targets government and policy organizations across Asia with Antino backdoor
item.description:
China-nexus UAT-11587 hits Asian governments with Antino, a Rust backdoor that hides C2 traffic inside Microsoft 365, reaching roughly 350 endpoints across eight countries over ten months.
Key findings:
- The five-stage infection chain starts with a spear-phishing email spoofed via SMTP envelope/From-header misalignment through Migadu using osc-cdn[.]com, paired with a cloned Gmail attachment widget pointing to Cloudflare Pages URLs like my-3lyt6wcp.pages[.]dev. mshta.exe runs the HTA stager, which beacons to a tracking endpoint at oisadjfoinsiduhfnoisdnfosdnoifnsoid.pages[.]dev, then pulls RC4-encrypted JScript from Cloudflare R2 or d2nq35tel3ucuo.cloudfront[.]net. That JScript exploits unsafe BinaryFormatter deserialization using an ActivitySurrogateSelector gadget chain to load TestAssembly.dll (GUID b2b3adb0-1669-4b94-86cb-6dd682ddbea3 in its AssemblyAttribute) directly into mshta.exe, which then sideloads slc.dll (Antino) via the legitimate Microsoft-signed ADK binary GatherOsState.exe.
- Antino is a Rust-compiled Windows backdoor (32-bit and 64-bit, DLL and standalone forms) that stores its config XOR-encrypted with alternating key 0xAB 0xCD in a custom PE section named .cfg. It communicates exclusively through Microsoft Graph, polling an attacker-controlled Outlook mailbox every 10 seconds for JSON command messages prefixed command_req_[session_id] and uploading heartbeat JSON to OneDrive at /antino/heartbeats/{session_id}.json every minute. All C2 traffic terminates at graph[.]microsoft[.]com and login.microsoftonline[.]com, making it nearly invisible in enterprise network logs. Persistence lands as an HKCU Run value pointing to files staged under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Windows GatherOSStateKit\, written via a PowerShell script executed through the legitimate Windows Scripted Diagnostics workflow: sdiagnhost.exe -Embedding runs result.ps1 via COM class CLSID {1F3D8AA5-9EBF-4EE4-85C2-EA40379AEDE8}.
- The load_shellcode command supports a sleep-mask evasion technique: Antino hooks Sleep and VirtualAlloc, marks the loaded payload region PAGE_READWRITE, encrypts it in place while the thread sleeps, then decrypts and restores permissions via a vectored exception handler on execution fault. This narrows the window for memory scanner detections against the secondary payload. Standalone fake-installer builds were served from microsoft-flash[.]com and wps-cn[.]com (historical IP 103.27.110[.]220).
- Attribution rests on multiple converging indicators: decoy documents carry the zh-CN language tag, Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 author metadata, and +08:00 timestamps; ten Antino build outputs reference rsproxy[.]cn in Cargo registry paths; PDB paths follow GitHub Actions Windows runner structure at D:\a\antino\antino\; and a JavaScript downloader shared infrastructure with CloudFront domain d32tpl7xt7175h.cloudfront[.]net previously linked to Chinese 🇨🇳 UNC6384 delivery activity.
- Scope: at least 16 affected or targeted institutional environments confirmed by July 2026, approximately 350 compromised endpoints across Taiwan 🇹🇼, India 🇮🇳, the Philippines 🇵🇭, Cambodia 🇰🇭, Pakistan 🇵🇰, Thailand 🇹🇭, Myanmar 🇲🇲, and Syria. Targets span defense, executive government, foreign affairs, legislative institutions, and civil society.
Hunt priority: look for GatherOsState.exe executing from user-writable directories outside its legitimate ADK install path, slc.dll loaded alongside it, and mshta.exe or wscript.exe making HTTPS connections to r2[.]dev or pages[.]dev subdomains. On the C2 side, hunt OAuth client-credentials flows to login.microsoftonline[.]com followed by Graph API calls to mail and OneDrive endpoints from non-interactive service contexts. The TestAssembly.dll GUID b2b3adb0-1669-4b94-86cb-6dd682ddbea3 is a reliable tooling-level pivot. Full IOC list, hashes, defanged URLs, ClamAV signatures, and Snort rules (Snort 2 and 3: 1:66880, 1:66881, 1:66882) are in the Talos report and their GitHub IOC repository.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2105236777191493882
