item.title: WHIPSHOT and SLAPSHOT: the tools behind an active Citrix NetScaler campaign
item.description:
CVE-2026-88772 (CVSS 9.5) in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway is being actively exploited as a zero-day, deploying novel web shells WHIPSHOT and SLAPSHOT across government, finance, education, and legal orgs.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88772 is a pre-authentication heap memory overflow triggered during the DTLS handshake, before any login is required. DTLS is enabled by default on NetScaler Gateway VPN virtual servers, making a large portion of exposed appliances vulnerable. A second zero-day, CVE-2026-88771, is being exploited alongside it. Exploitation has been observed in the wild since at least early September 2026 across North America and Europe.
- The exploit fingerprint lives in the logs. Look for SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE events tagged DTLSv1.0 with "Handshake failure-Internal Error" combined with a packet engine process crash and a failed watchdog restart occurring close together in time. That pairing is the strongest on-appliance indicator that exploitation was attempted or successful.
- Post-exploitation tradecraft is deliberate and evasion-focused. The attacker modifies httpd.conf to treat .deb or .sig files as executable PHP, then drops WHIPSHOT disguised as a Debian package. A redirect maps an innocent-looking .ico request (e.g. /vpn/media/e6ee7c85.ico) to the hidden .sig shell. WHIPSHOT reads commands from sequential HTTP headers, decodes Base64, routes over loopback, suppresses error output, and always returns HTTP 404, leaving web server logs clean on the surface. Requests that return 404 but take unusually long to complete are a hunting signal.
- SLAPSHOT is a Python TCP proxy that opens a local port and tunnels traffic into the internal network, effectively turning the perimeter appliance into a pivot point. It is self-cleaning: idle sessions close after 15 minutes and the tool deletes its own port and lock files after 10 minutes of inactivity, a deliberate anti-forensic design. In at least one confirmed intrusion it was used for internal network reconnaissance and credential harvesting.
- Persistence is maintained by setting /bin/sh setuid root so that subsequent web shell commands continue to run with root privileges, followed by a forced appliance reboot to lock in the change. Assume that every credential the appliance ever handled (admin accounts, SSH keys, TLS certificates, LDAP and RADIUS credentials) is compromised. Rotate after patching, not before.
Practitioner takeaway: if you are investigating a potentially compromised NetScaler, start with the ns.log and /var/nslog/ for the SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE and packet engine crash pairing, then audit httpd.conf for unexpected MIME-type mappings. Hunt /netscaler/ns_gui/ and /var/vpn/ for .deb, .sig, and .ico files with recent modification times. Check /bin/sh permissions for the setuid bit. If DTLS cannot be patched out immediately, disable it and block inbound UDP/443 as a partial mitigant, but patch CVE-2026-88771 separately. The full IOC list and technical indicators are in the Mandiant and GTIG report.

item.title: Custom ChatGPTs push ClickFix attacks to deploy RAT malware
item.description:
A novel ClickFix campaign abuses OpenAI's custom GPT feature and Google-sponsored ads to deliver a full-featured RAT, with persistence surviving deletion via a homemade encrypted file system.
Key findings:
- The threat actor created a malicious custom GPT named "Plus 5.6" on the legitimate ChatGPT[.]com domain and promoted it through sponsored Google search results. The GPT directed victims to a Google Sites page displaying a fake Cloudflare verification, instructing them to run a PowerShell command. Using both ChatGPT[.]com and Google Sites as delivery infrastructure lends the attack significant legitimacy, raising the likelihood victims comply. At least 40 incidents connecting to the Google Sites page were investigated, with two confirmed involving the custom GPT variant directly.
- The PowerShell command silently launches an MSI from the temp folder via msiexec.exe, which drops a legitimate signed application alongside a modified DLL that side-loads the RAT. The campaign initially used a Canon-signed host application, later pivoting to a Stardock-signed one while retaining the same payload. This signed-binary abuse is the core evasion mechanism: the malicious DLL rides behind a trusted executable identity.
- The RAT supports remote desktop access, audio and camera capture, file search, host reconnaissance, and execution of additional payloads. For persistence, it writes a Registry Run key and a scheduled task, both named "Canon Configuration Reader." If either artifact is deleted, they reappear, a sign of active watchdog logic in the infection chain.
- Phase 6 of the chain is the most forensically notable: the attackers built a custom encrypted archive with its own folder tree, a 1,128-entry index recording parent paths, file sizes, and per-file encryption keys, followed by packed file contents. This is not a standard encrypted blob; it is a purpose-built obfuscated file system designed to conceal the persistence script and RAT from file-based detection. Most of the infection chain runs in memory or behind files that appear benign on disk.
Detection and response: Hunt for PowerShell spawning msiexec.exe with silent install flags pointing to %Temp%. Inspect %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ for signed executables running from non-standard subdirectories. Check both the Run key and scheduled tasks for the name "Canon Configuration Reader" and treat their reappearance after deletion as confirmation of active persistence. The Huntress report includes a set of detection opportunities grounded in process activity monitoring; full details are in the report.

item.title: The Developer is the New Perimeter: How Supply Chain Attacks Are Becoming Cloud Breaches
item.description:
Supply chain attacks from Sep 2025 through May 2026 show a repeating kill chain: malicious packages steal cloud credentials at install time, before any application code runs, turning developer machines and CI/CD pipelines into cloud breach entry points.
Key findings:
- Three named campaigns define the pattern. Shai-Hulud (emerging September 2025) injected worm code into popular npm packages including [@]ctrl/tinycolor, exfiltrating credentials to attacker-controlled GitHub repos. Its May 2026 Mini variant hit 639 package versions across 323 [@]antv packages, including echarts-for-react at 1.1 million weekly downloads, targeting GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, KUBECONFIG, and VAULT_TOKEN via the preinstall lifecycle hook. Credentials were stolen even when the install was cancelled after the hook fired.
- BufferZoneCorp (Ruby gems and Go modules) went further than credential theft: it redirected GOPROXY, disabled checksum verification, dropped fake go binary wrappers into the CI runner PATH (T1574.007), and appended attacker SSH public keys to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (T1098.004), meaning the build host itself was modified for persistent access. TeamPCP compromised Trivy, Checkmarx KICS, LiteLLM, and a Telnyx library, then bypassed GitHub secret masking by reading runner process memory directly and used stolen PATs to force-push malicious commits across version tags.
- The credential harvest targets are predictable and plaintext: ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, .npmrc, .netrc, and SSH key files (T1552.001, T1552.004). Once credentials reach the attacker, the documented post-compromise cloud activity includes IAM reconnaissance, EC2/Lambda/S3 enumeration (T1526), S3 data exfiltration (T1530), and IMDS probing for temporary instance credentials (T1552.005). UNC6426 escalated from a compromised nx npm package to AWS admin access in 72 hours.
- The IMDS attack surface is underappreciated here. Most of these payloads probe 169.254.169.254 with simple GET requests, which IMDSv2 blocks by requiring a session-token PUT first. AWS Config rule ec2-imdsv2-check and an SCP preventing IMDSv1 instance launches directly cuts off this vector. Where CI/CD runners have no legitimate reason to query the metadata endpoint, egress filtering on 169.254.169.254 raises the bar further.
- April 21-23, 2026 saw npm, PyPI, and Docker Hub hit within 48 hours: the trojaned [@]bitwarden/cli package and compromised Checkmarx KICS images shared C2 infrastructure and propagated via stolen publishing tokens. On May 28, 14 typosquatting npm packages impersonating OpenSearch and ElasticSearch libraries used stolen publish tokens to infect additional maintainer-owned packages, confirming that stolen ecosystem credentials extend the blast radius beyond the initial victim.
Practitioner takeaway: Package removal is not containment. When a CI/CD runner executes an unvetted package, treat every credential and token that runner could access as potentially exposed. Pull CloudTrail, GCP Cloud Audit Logs, or Azure Monitor for the full exposure window and look for API calls matching T1526 and T1530 patterns: IAM enumeration, new role creation, S3 ListBuckets, GetObject, and Lambda or Secrets Manager access using the affected credential. Rotate or revoke before investigating, not after. For prevention, enforce ignore-scripts=true in CI .npmrc, pin dependencies with lockfile integrity checks, and replace long-lived stored keys with short-lived OIDC-based credentials. The full MITRE ATT&CK mapping is in the report.

item.title: The PaperPhone Cluster: One Operator, 80K IPs, 43 countries
item.description:
A single scraping operator running 80K IPs across 43 countries is exposed as a coordinated bot cluster hiding behind fabricated geolocation, spoofed mobile identities, and a deliberately fragmented IP portfolio designed to defeat traditional blocklisting.
Key findings:
- CrowdSec's alpha bot detection feature, shipped in v1.8.0, surfaced the cluster dubbed "PaperPhone" within two weeks of community deployment. 75,000 IPs spread across 230 IP blocks and 80 networks are involved. The infrastructure predates discovery, with IPs progressively joining as more sensors came online and IP rotation accelerating as banned addresses cycled out. The full breadth only became visible because the detection layer shifted from "what is this IP doing" to "what is the client behind this IP actually running", a meaningful investigative pivot.
- Geographic diversity is manufactured, not real. Traffic claims to originate from 43 countries, but request timing betrays a single operator timezone. Japan 🇯🇵 peaks at 05:00 local with 18.7% night-share, India 🇮🇳 peaks at 01:00 with 18.5%. Synchronization across regions 13 to 14 hours apart (Japan 🇯🇵/US, Australia 🇦🇺/Canada) collapses when viewed in UTC, exposing a single coordinated pulse. IP blocks reinforce this: adjacent /23s in the same /22 are artificially geolocated to Brussels, Bangkok, Tokyo, and Paris, a deliberate fragmentation pattern repeated across all 230 blocks. WHOIS inconsistencies compound it, with ranges showing mismatched RIRs, registrant countries, and claimed geolocations simultaneously.
- Bot fingerprinting uncovered consistent lies at the browser layer. The cluster cycles through exactly 13 device identities: 5 Android variants (Pixel 9, Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, others) and 7 iOS variants. Every single bot, regardless of claimed device, reported a 375x812 viewport matching iPhone 10/11 only, and every browser returned Google SwiftShader as the WebGL renderer via UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL. SwiftShader is a CPU-based software renderer used when no GPU is available. Modern flagship Android hardware essentially never triggers it, and iOS devices run WebKit, making a SwiftShader signal on claimed iOS 14/15 technically impossible.
- M247 does not own the IP blocks but routes more than 20% of PaperPhone's traffic as transit provider. A small number of controlling entities own the majority of the 230 blocks, with ranges showing inter-regional transfers as recently as 2025 to obscure lineage. Block utilization density shows most ranges were used at or near full capacity during scraping operations, ruling out coincidental residential overlap and confirming this is purpose-built datacenter infrastructure dressed up as organic global traffic.
Practitioner takeaway: geoblocking fails against operators who manufacture geographic identity at the IP registration layer. The detection surface that actually works here is client-side behavioral fingerprinting: viewport dimensions, WebGL renderer strings, and timezone-to-request-time correlation. For threat hunters, UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL returning SwiftShader on claimed mobile user agents is a high-confidence bot signal worth building into WAF and SIEM detection logic. When investigating scraping clusters, cross-reference AS ownership graphs against transit providers, not just WHOIS registrant country, because M247 routing 20% of traffic without owning a single block shows how transit-layer attribution matters. Full cluster data and IOC context are in the CrowdSec report.

item.title: No MDM for Linux? A 68-line Elastic workflow keeps every endpoint's config current
item.description:
Elastic Security Labs built a 68-line YAML workflow that turns a one-shot Elastic Defend response action into a full reconciliation loop for Linux endpoints with no MDM coverage, checking state before acting and skipping duplicates automatically.
Key findings:
- The workflow solves a real MDM gap: most enterprise MDM platforms cover macOS and Windows but leave Linux workstations unmanaged. Rather than a cron job that blindly queues repeat actions against offline hosts, the workflow asks two questions per endpoint before touching anything: does this host need the deployment, and is an identical action already queued? The pending-action query filters on the exact script ID stored in consts, so two independent deployments with different script IDs deduplicate independently and never suppress each other.
- The full loop is five YAML capabilities chained together: a scheduled trigger fires every six hours, a kibana.request step lists Linux endpoints via KQL against the united.agent.local_metadata namespace (not host.os.type, which returns nothing there), a foreach iterates each endpoint, a data.filter matches pending runscript actions by script ID, and an if/else either logs a skip or fires the run_script POST to /api/endpoint/action/run_script. A newly enrolled laptop is caught on the next pass. A host offline for a week accumulates one queued action, not one per cycle. Actions expire after two weeks, so a persistently dark host gets a fresh action when it returns.
- The distro filter in the kuery is a silent exclusion risk that responders and deployment engineers need to internalize. The workflow queries for debian, redhat, arch, suse, and fedora families only. Gentoo, Alpine, and Amazon Linux hosts produce no error and receive no deployment. If your fleet includes those distros, the workflow will never tell you they were skipped. Audit your fleet composition against the kuery before treating coverage as complete.
- Permissions and secret handling carry real operational risk. Scheduled workflows run with the privileges of the user who last saved them, and saving the workflow mints a stored API key for that principal. Deactivating or re-roling the account does not invalidate the key: the schedule continues running with the previously captured access. Refreshing or revoking that access requires an authorized user to resave the workflow or toggle it off and on. The execution principal holds Execute Operations over every Elastic Defend-covered host, so scope it narrowly. Secrets embedded in script library entries (the report notes an OTel ingest credential lives there) are visible to anyone with Elastic Defend Scripts Management access, which is a separate privilege from the scheduled execution principal.
- The pattern generalizes beyond AI coding agent config. The YAML owns when and where a deployment runs; the script library entry owns what it changes. Any idempotently written, non-zero-on-failure script drops into this loop without touching the workflow. The report calls out certificate renewal, EDR config drift remediation, and credential rotation nudges as immediate reuse candidates across any OS Elastic Defend covers.
DFIR takeaway: if you are investigating an endpoint that runs Elastic Defend and you see unexpected runscript actions in Response Actions History, check the associated script ID against the script library and review which workflow principal triggered it and when. The execution history in Kibana shows why one host received an action and an adjacent host did not, which is exactly the audit trail a responder needs to distinguish legitimate reconciliation from an adversary abusing a high-privilege workflow execution account. Verify the stored API key's originating principal has not been tampered with by checking who last saved the workflow.

item.title: Phishing Abuses RMM Tools for Persistent Access
item.description:
Phishing campaigns observed in July 2026 abused legitimate MSP360 RMM and ConnectWise ScreenConnect to build redundant remote access channels, then dropped credential-harvesting and visibility-reduction tooling across multiple industries.
Key findings:
- Initial access came via phishing links directing victims to actor-controlled pages impersonating Zoom, Google Meet, Adobe Reader, DHL, and document-signing portals (T1566.002, T1204). The payload, a legitimate digitally signed MSP360 RMM v2.5.0.67 installer (SHA256: 108ef7e628d7a20bd6241a5b57149e27a6061f467123eb64061975559f8f73dc), was hosted across attacker infrastructure and legitimate cloud services including Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, GitLab, and Supabase. Filenames were crafted to mimic business content, examples include VIP_ECARD_INVITATION_rmm_v2.5.0.67.exe and ZoomSetup_Installation_v2.5.0.67.exe.
- After UAC elevation succeeded, the installer dropped components to C:\Program Files\RMM Agent\, registered two persistent services (RMM.Agent.exe and RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe, T1543.003), wrote Registry Run keys for tray components (T1547.001), and opened an inbound Windows Firewall allow rule for UDP port 48678 on RMM.Agent.exe. The installer logged its own progress via eventcreate.exe under the source "MSP360 RMM Agent installer," producing "Begin installation" and "End installation. MSP360 de Success." events, a direct artifact for timeline reconstruction.
- RMM.Agent.exe then launched PowerShell, modified execution policy, used Invoke-WebRequest to pull ClientSetup.msi from actor-controlled infrastructure, and installed ConnectWise ScreenConnect silently via msiexec.exe /qn (T1218.007, T1059.001). ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe and ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe were registered as services, establishing a second independent remote access channel. The threat actor is unattributed. Microsoft also observed FaronicsDeployAgent.exe used identically as an alternative first-stage RMM to install ScreenConnect, confirming the technique is not MSP360-specific.
- Post-compromise tooling was staged to C:\Users\%user%\OneDrive\Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp\ and C:\Users\%user%\Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp\ via ScreenConnect's RunFile functionality. Delivered utilities included WebBrowserPassView.exe, WebBrowserBookmarksView.exe, DefenderControl.exe, SCHider.exe, HideMouse.exe, and variants named to mimic Windows Defender and Phone Link components (T1036.005). The full list of 25 post-compromise tool hashes and 7 ScreenConnect C2 domains, including adswre[.]cfd, trews[.]cfd, and sdfghj.rd-team[.]ru, is in the report.
Practitioner takeaway: three KQL hunting queries are in the report covering MSP360 SHA256 presence in DeviceFileEvents, RMM.Agent.exe spawning PowerShell in DeviceProcessEvents, and ScreenConnect network connections correlating back to actor infrastructure. Start there, then pivot to the eventcreate.exe log entries (source: MSP360 RMM Agent installer) in the System event log and check for new inbound firewall rules on UDP 48678. Verify any ScreenConnect Temp staging directories for the named utilities. If MSP360 or an unrecognized RMM is present, treat any account used during installation as compromised and rotate credentials immediately. Full IOC list is in the report.

The installer logged its own progress via eventcreate.exe under the source "MSP360 RMM Agent installer," producing "Begin installation" and "End installation. MSP360 de Success." events, a direct artifact for timeline reconstruction.

- RMM.Agent.exe then launched PowerShell, modified execution policy, used Invoke-WebRequest to pull ClientSetup.msi from actor-controlled infrastructure, and installed ConnectWise ScreenConnect silently via msiexec.exe /qn (T1218.007, T1059.001). ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe and ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe were registered as services, establishing a second independent remote access channel. The threat actor is unattributed. Microsoft also observed FaronicsDeployAgent.exe used identically as an alternative first-stage RMM to install ScreenConnect, confirming the technique is not MSP360-specific.

- Post-compromise tooling was staged to C:\Users\%user%\OneDrive\Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp\ and C:\Users\%user%\Documents\ScreenConnect\Temp\ via ScreenConnect's RunFile functionality. Delivered utilities included WebBrowserPassView.exe, WebBrowserBookmarksView.exe, DefenderControl.exe, SCHider.exe, HideMouse.exe, and variants named to mimic Windows Defender and Phone Link components (T1036.005). The full list of 25 post-compromise tool hashes and 7 ScreenConnect C2 domains, including adswre[.]cfd, trews[.]cfd, and sdfghj.rd-team[.]ru, is in the report.

Practitioner takeaway: three KQL hunting queries are in the report covering MSP360 SHA256 presence in DeviceFileEvents, RMM.Agent.exe spawning PowerShell in DeviceProcessEvents, and ScreenConnect network connections correlating back to actor infrastructure. Start there, then pivot to the eventcreate.exe log entries (source: MSP360 RMM Agent installer) in the System event log and check for new inbound firewall rules on UDP 48678. Verify any ScreenConnect Temp staging directories for the named utilities. If MSP360 or an unrecognized RMM is present, treat any account used during installation as compromised and rotate credentials immediately. Full IOC list is in the report.

item.title: Star Blizzard scales phishing operations with RedFlick malware delivery
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 Star Blizzard scales up phishing with a new RedFlick delivery chain, deploying the CosmicPulse backdoor across 100+ organizations in at least 13 campaigns targeting Ukraine-linked entities in the US 🇺🇸 and UK.
Key findings:
- Star Blizzard shifted from tight spear-phishing to broader engagement campaigns in 2026, first sending clean, attachment-free emails to build rapport, then following up after a reply with a password-protected RAR or ZIP archive. The archive password arrives as an image inside the message body, bypassing text-based inspection. Targets span government, diplomacy, research, public policy, journalism, and financial sectors with connections to Ukraine 🇺🇦.
- The archive contains VHDX files or LNK files disguised as PDF documents. Execution launches scripts and legitimate Windows utilities that pull additional components from attacker-controlled infrastructure. Beginning in April 2026, RedFlick installers created scheduled tasks, collected basic host information, enabled WebDAV access, and staged components used to install the CosmicPulse backdoor for persistent access.
- In July 2026, Star Blizzard added another layer: a password-protected RAR nested inside a ZIP. The enclosed shortcut downloaded a PDF with encoded data that PowerShell extracted and executed to retrieve an MSI installer. Microsoft confirmed RedFlick communicating with remote infrastructure, creating scheduled tasks, and deploying CosmicPulse in at least one confirmed incident.
- The technique is designed to exploit normal business workflows. Conference invitations, policy discussions, research collaboration, and document-sharing requests give the malware delivery stage cover as a routine exchange. Recipients who have already replied are filtered as engaged targets before any malicious payload is introduced, raising the likelihood of successful execution.
- The infection chain offers multiple detection checkpoints on the endpoint even when the archive itself cannot be inspected: archive extraction, VHDX mounting, LNK execution, PowerShell spawning from unusual parents, WebDAV activity, MSI installs, scheduled-task creation, and outbound connections to unfamiliar external infrastructure. Correlating these events in sequence reveals the RedFlick chain more reliably than attachment scanning alone.
Hunt in email telemetry for password-protected archives arriving in thread context after an earlier attachment-free message, then pivot to the endpoint. Look for the VHDX mount, LNK or MSI execution, PowerShell network retrievals, and newly created scheduled tasks in close temporal proximity. If execution is confirmed, isolate the host, preserve the full email thread and original archive, enumerate all scheduled tasks and persistence mechanisms, collect process and network telemetry, and review the affected user's mailbox rules, active sessions, and recent communications for signs of follow-on targeting or lateral movement.

item.title: Zilliz / Attu | 2.6.5
item.description:
Attu 2.6.5 ships two chained flaws: unauthenticated SSRF plus a case-sensitive regex bypass that together hand an attacker full administrative control of the Kubernetes namespace where Attu is deployed, including live AWS IAM credentials.
Key findings:
- The first flaw, rated Critical, lives in the Playground feature's server-side middleware at /app/dist/src/middleware/index.js. The authorization check gates on the presence of a milvus-client-id header: if that header is absent, the milvusClientId variable evaluates to an empty string, which JavaScript treats as false, and the entire auth block is skipped. The playground controller at /app/dist/src/playground/playground.controller.js compounds this by not validating clientId presence before calling makeRequest. A bare POST to /api/v1/playground with no milvus-client-id header and a target in the host field is all that is needed to turn any internet-exposed Attu instance into an open HTTP/HTTPS proxy.
- The second flaw, rated High, is a case-sensitive regular expression in playground.service.js that classifies a URL scheme as absolute only when it matches /^[a-z][a-z\d\+\-\.]*:/. Supplying a mixed-case scheme like HTTP:// or hTtp:// causes Attu to treat the url parameter as a relative path and route security validation against the public host parameter instead. The Axios library Attu calls internally uses a case-insensitive regex for the same check, so it happily treats the url value as an absolute URL and connects to whatever private address is embedded there, including 169.254.169.254[.]
- Bishop Fox chained both flaws against an Attu container running in an AWS EKS cluster using the official zilliz/attu:v2.6.5 image. They reached the IMDSv2 endpoint at hxxp://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token/ unauthenticated, retrieved a session token, then pulled temporary IAM credentials tied to the eksctl-milvus-eks-cluster-nodegrou-NodeInstanceRole-CT8qI3ybezSz EC2 node role. Those credentials authenticated directly to the Kubernetes API server (public access was enabled by default in the Milvus EKS deployment guide), giving them system:node membership in the cluster.
- From the node identity, Bishop Fox enumerated pods and service accounts on the node, minted a token for the over-privileged milvus-demo-pulsarv3-broker-acct service account (namespace-wide create/modify rights in the milvus namespace), then deployed a privileged pod with hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, and a host-path volume mount of /. The pod executed a reverse shell, landing root on the underlying EC2 node and full access to secrets across the milvus namespace.
- Version 2.6.5 will not receive a patch. The vendor confirmed the 2.6.x line is end-of-life and recommends upgrading to Attu 3.0.0, released September 3, 2026, which is a full backend rewrite where neither flaw is reproducible. If immediate upgrade is blocked, isolate Attu behind an authenticated reverse proxy, restrict or remove the pod's IMDSv2 access (IMDSv2 hop-limit of 1 blocks container access to the metadata service), apply least-privilege RBAC to the Attu service account, and audit any service account in the namespace for create-pod or create-token permissions that could enable the same privilege escalation path.
For incident responders: if you are investigating a potentially compromised EKS cluster running Attu 2.6.5, check Kubernetes audit logs for unexpected kubectl create token calls against service accounts in the milvus namespace, pod creation events with hostNetwork or privileged securityContext, and AWS CloudTrail for sts:GetCallerIdentity or ec2:DescribeInstances calls originating from the node IAM role outside normal operational windows. IMDS access from within a container that has no legitimate reason to query 169.254.169.254 is a reliable anomaly signal. Full vulnerability details and proof-of-concept request chains are in the Bishop Fox report.

item.title: Digital Forensics: iOS Forensics: Basics
item.description:
iOS forensics fundamentals explained through the lens of encryption classes, BFU/AFU state, and the 72-hour reboot window introduced in iOS 18.1, with practical guidance on extraction methods and key artifacts.
Key findings:
- File protection classes are the foundation of every iOS acquisition decision. Class A data (mail bodies) re-encrypts when the screen locks. Class C, where app data, chats, and photo libraries live, unlocks on first passcode entry after reboot and stays accessible even through screen locks until the next reboot. Class D uses a device-only key and never needs a passcode. Knowing which class holds your target data tells you whether an AFU phone is enough or whether you needed to be faster.
- BFU vs. AFU is not a tool limitation, it is a hardware reality. BFU gives triage-level output at best: device info, iOS version, thin metadata. AFU opens Class C and analysts estimate that gets you roughly 95% of a full dump. No toolset, including Cellebrite Inseyets or its predecessor suite (Premium, PA7), changes this equation on current hardware. Brute-force passcode support is limited to specific older models on specific iOS versions, not a blanket capability.
- Since iOS 18.1, a phone sitting idle for roughly 72 hours reboots itself with no user-configurable override. Labs have already seen properly isolated AFU phones drop back to BFU in storage. A Faraday bag is not a long-term holding solution anymore: document the phone's state at seizure, get it into acquisition fast, and treat the clock as evidence-critical.
- Pairing records created when a user tapped "Trust This Computer" live on the host machine and can allow a lab system to communicate with a locked AFU phone without a new unlock, but only before USB Restricted Mode fires (roughly one hour after the phone locks). Every computer the subject owned is therefore a secondary evidence source. Lockdown Mode is a separate hardening feature: toggling it reboots the phone and destroys AFU state. The report cites a 2026 case where Lockdown Mode prevented extraction of a seized reporter's powered-on iPhone.
- The artifacts that matter most are the ones investigators most commonly miss. Always collect WAL and SHM files alongside SQLite databases for iMessage, WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram: deleted rows often remain in the freelist or WAL until a vacuum runs. KnowledgeC and its successor Biome log app-in-focus events, unlock events, notifications, and web activity, enabling screen-state reconstruction. PowerLog confirms the device was powered and connected at a given time. Photos.sqlite covers hidden, recently deleted images, and iCloud sync state. On modern iPhones there is no unallocated space to carve for deleted iMessages: the key is destroyed and the database is cleaned up later, any claim of raw-flash iMessage recovery on current hardware deserves hard scrutiny.
Practitioner takeaway: at seizure, immediately document BFU or AFU state and timestamp it. If AFU, treat 72 hours as your hard acquisition deadline and do not rely on Faraday storage to preserve that state. Before touching the phone, locate and preserve pairing records from every associated computer. During analysis, pull KnowledgeC/Biome and PowerLog from the full file system image alongside every chat database's WAL and SHM files: those behavioral stores and transaction logs are where timeline reconstruction actually happens.

item.title: ​​Beyond source code: A path to the keys to the kingdom
item.description:
Storm-3068 turned a self-service password reset into full access across Azure DevOps, Kubernetes clusters, and cloud infrastructure, without touching a single piece of malware.
Key findings:
- Initial access came through a self-service password reset, after which Storm-3068 registered its own authentication methods to the compromised account, locking in persistent identity control. No exploit, no phishing payload: just an abused account recovery workflow that handed the attacker a fully owned identity.
- Azure DevOps was the pivot point. The threat actor used legitimate administrative tools and automated scripts to enumerate repositories, projects, pipelines, and deployment environments. Because Azure DevOps sits at the intersection of identity, development, and cloud operations, it functioned as a roadmap to the broader environment, not just a code host.
- Storm-3068 built a malicious pipeline authorized to access more than 50 resources. The pipeline deployed a kube agent and executed jobs to harvest kubeconfig files containing cluster connection details and auth tokens. Seven stolen kubeconfig files were ultimately committed to a repository, giving the attacker direct credentials to targeted Kubernetes clusters.
- To maintain remote access, the threat actor modified pipeline scripts to install the Atera remote management agent and download the Chisel tunneling utility. Chisel was used to establish a reverse tunnel to an external IP, exposing the Kubernetes API server to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
- DART reconstructed the full attack chain using Azure DevOps audit logs and Git version history, two artifact sources that responders should treat as primary evidence in any DevOps-involved intrusion. Those logs revealed timeline, pipeline modifications, repository additions, and lateral movement paths that endpoint telemetry alone would have missed.
Takeaway: In any identity-driven cloud intrusion, pull Azure DevOps audit logs and full Git commit history early. Look for pipeline creation or modification events, newly registered authentication methods on user accounts, and kube agent deployments in build jobs. Hunt for Chisel or similar tunneling binaries dropped by pipeline runners, and review service connections for any that authenticate to more resources than the owning project justifies. Least-privilege pipeline permissions and phishing-resistant MFA on accounts with DevOps access are the structural controls this case argues for. The full report is available from Microsoft Security.

item.title: Ransomware Response Playbook for MSPs
item.description:
Ransomware hit 48% of all breaches in Verizon's 2026 DBIR, and MSPs are both first responders and targets. The first 90 minutes, the evidence you preserve, and the calls you make in sequence decide the outcome.
Key findings:
- The threat landscape has shifted decisively toward dual extortion: 70% of ransomware claims in Coalition's 2026 Cyber Claims Report involved encryption and data theft together. That means a clean restore does not close the incident. Notification obligations attach the moment data left the environment, regardless of whether decryption succeeds. Your playbook needs a forensics track and a legal track running in parallel with recovery from hour one, and the clock for both starts at discovery, not at containment.
- Evidence destruction is the most common and costly mistake in early response. CISA's guidance is explicit: isolate affected hosts, but do not power them down unless you cannot disconnect them from the network any other way. Volatile memory holds the loader, the injected process, and the operator's staging paths. Shutting a machine down or reimaging patient zero before imaging disk and memory destroys the initial access artifact, which is the answer the insurer needs to determine how the attacker got in. Use console-driven isolation, keep the endpoint agent alive, and capture memory and disk from a sample of affected devices before any recovery work begins.
- Notify the carrier before you engage a forensics firm. Most cyber policies require notice within a defined window and mandate that counsel and IR vendors come from an approved panel. Engaging your preferred firm before carrier authorization puts the client's cost recovery at risk. The carrier's claims number, the policy number, and the panel requirements belong in the client's runbook alongside the network diagram. On sanctions: OFAC's guidance since 2020, updated September 2021, makes clear that facilitating a ransom payment to a sanctioned entity carries strict liability, meaning civil penalties can attach even without knowledge that the counterparty was sanctioned. MSPs must never negotiate or transmit payment on a client's behalf, and the master services agreement should state that plainly.
- MSPs face a portfolio exposure unique to their position. Shared RMM agents, PSA integrations with API keys, delegated admin into customer Microsoft tenants, common backup appliances, and shared administrative accounts all create a single-compromise-to-many-clients path. CISA, NSA, and MS-ISAC warned about this vector in January 2023. When a client calls, check every tenant that shares infrastructure with them before declaring scope limited to the one that reported.
- Reporting deadlines are layered and tight. HIPAA gives a business associate 60 days from discovery to notify the covered entity. CISA is expected to finalize the CIRCIA reporting rule in September 2026, requiring 72 hours to report a covered incident and 24 hours to report a ransom payment. States add their own layer: Washington requires resident notification within 30 days and attorney general notice once a breach exceeds 500 residents. Log retention predating the incident is what makes these timelines defensible. If EDR telemetry rolled off at seven days and initial access was 40 days prior, no analyst hours recover that answer.
Practitioner takeaway: before the next engagement, write the declaration threshold in plain language, name the incident commander and the communication owner, and confirm log retention spans at least 90 days across every client environment. Identity remediation precedes server restoration: rotate service accounts, reset privileged credentials, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, re-enroll MFA for elevated accounts, and reset the Kerberos TGT account twice with a replication interval between resets before restoring any domain controller. Hunt for the same techniques post-recovery, not just the same indicators, and confirm the original access path is closed before formally closing the incident.

CISA, NSA, and MS-ISAC warned about this vector in January 2023. When a client calls, check every tenant that shares infrastructure with them before declaring scope limited to the one that reported.

- Reporting deadlines are layered and tight. HIPAA gives a business associate 60 days from discovery to notify the covered entity. CISA is expected to finalize the CIRCIA reporting rule in September 2026, requiring 72 hours to report a covered incident and 24 hours to report a ransom payment. States add their own layer: Washington requires resident notification within 30 days and attorney general notice once a breach exceeds 500 residents. Log retention predating the incident is what makes these timelines defensible. If EDR telemetry rolled off at seven days and initial access was 40 days prior, no analyst hours recover that answer.

Practitioner takeaway: before the next engagement, write the declaration threshold in plain language, name the incident commander and the communication owner, and confirm log retention spans at least 90 days across every client environment. Identity remediation precedes server restoration: rotate service accounts, reset privileged credentials, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, re-enroll MFA for elevated accounts, and reset the Kerberos TGT account twice with a replication interval between resets before restoring any domain controller. Hunt for the same techniques post-recovery, not just the same indicators, and confirm the original access path is closed before formally closing the incident.

item.title: From AI Agents to RCE - Building a Vulnerability Research Workflow
item.description:
AI-assisted workflow chains two FreeRDP bugs into client-side RCE in four days on a half-million-line C codebase, demonstrating that agentic tooling can compress serious research timelines without eliminating the researcher.
Key findings:
- Quarkslab's harness runs an eight-stage pipeline: graph, recon, slicing, analysis, triage, PoC, chain, exploit. A deterministic core indexes the target (13,506 functions, 3,105 types, 31,705 call edges for FreeRDP at commit 993499447) and runs static taint to attacker-controlled sinks. AI agents sit above that layer to form hypotheses, filter noise, and drive toward a PoC. The core is tuned for recall on purpose: it over-produces so the agent layer absorbs the noise before a researcher ever sees it.
- Two vulnerabilities were confirmed. First: a routing-token heap overflow in libfreerdp/core/nego.c. A malicious server sends a LoadBalanceInfo payload via Server Redirection PDU. FreeRDP stores that length in nego->RoutingTokenLength with no equivalent size restriction to the one guarding the direct protocol path. At Stream_Write inside nego_send_negotiation_request (nego.c:1083/1098), a 615-byte token is copied into a 512-byte heap allocation. ASan confirmed the write: "heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 615" reached through rdp_client_redirect. Critically, this only fires with WITH_VERBOSE_WINPR_ASSERT=OFF, the default on Debian and Ubuntu builds. Second: a heap disclosure in channels/urbdrc/client/data_transfer. An error in a USB-redirection completion path leaves attacker-supplied OutputBufferSize in place with no data written, and the client later uses that size when emitting the response, leaking heap contents. ASan heap-fill validation confirmed 64 bytes of 0xcd pattern in the emitted PDU.
- The chaining stage combined both: the overflow provides a blind attacker-controlled heap write; the USB disclosure provides visibility into heap contents. A server redirection can force reconnect and trigger the write after the session is established. That composition made RCE plausible. The agent automated layout hypothesis testing and harness generation, but researcher intervention was required twice during exploitation: once to derive the libc base from the leak and once to compose the final payload. The result was ASLR defeat and code execution confirmed by /tmp/pwned.
- The pipeline processed 130 findings from the two slices discussed, reduced them to 36 clusters, and confirmed 20 as real and reachable. The two exploitable findings came from slices ranked 166th and 109th out of 304, reinforcing that automated ranking is a search-space map, not a verdict. The report also contextualises the threat: one operator breached nine Mexican 🇲🇽 government agencies using Claude Code and GPT-4.1 across 305 servers, exfiltrating close to 200 million records. The ratio was five commands executed per instruction typed. Agentic tooling does not raise the skill ceiling; it raises the work-per-operator ceiling.
Hunt priority: if you maintain or monitor FreeRDP-based clients (Remmina, GNOME Connections, KRDC, Apache Guacamole's guacd), check whether WITH_VERBOSE_WINPR_ASSERT is disabled in your builds, because that silent difference is what allows the heap write to reach memcpy. Review server-redirection flows in network logs for abnormally large LoadBalanceInfo payloads and unexpected reconnect sequences mid-session. Both advisories (routing token heap overflow and USB redirection heap disclosure) have been filed with the FreeRDP maintainers. Check the report for advisory links and the full exploitation walk-through to understand what post-connection artifacts the chain leaves behind.

item.title: Inside The Com: Understanding the Ecosystem Behind Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, ShinyHunters, and FALCON
item.description:
The Com ecosystem explained: how LAPSUS$, Scattered Spider, ShinyHunters, and the emerging Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters brand share infrastructure, TTPs, and members, making actor attribution secondary to behavioral defense.
Key findings:
- The Com is not a single threat actor. It is a decentralized, English-speaking cybercriminal substrate organized around loosely affiliated crews that share social-engineering tradecraft, rebrand freely, and recruit across Telegram and Discord. The financially motivated pillar has produced LAPSUS$, Scattered Spider, and ShinyHunters. The August 2025 emergence of Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters (SLH) demonstrates that convergence: a merged brand running the Sh1nySp1d3r RaaS, linked to Silent Ransom Group, and claiming intrusions at SoundCloud, Betterment, and Crunchbase in 2026. SLH has also been observed exploiting CVE-2025-61882, a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability, during intrusions.
- The shared TTP table in the report is the most operationally useful piece for defenders. Initial access is almost always social engineering: vishing and help-desk impersonation (Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, FALCON), SIM swapping (Beige, Star Fraud, LAPSUS$, Scattered Spider), and AitM phishing via passkey- or SSO-themed domains (FALCON and sibling brands Redact, Pink, Helix). Once in, the playbook shifts to MFA bombing, OAuth token abuse against Salesforce and Salesloft, and bulk exfiltration from SharePoint, OneDrive, and Box via automated scripts. Ransomware is rented, not built: ALPHV/BlackCat, DragonForce, Qilin, and Sh1nySp1d3r have all been used as RaaS partners.
- Domain infrastructure patterns are a practical hunt pivot. Scattered Spider registers phishing domains in the format organization-sso[.]com, organization-okta[.]com, and organization-helpdesk[.]com. ReliaQuest found 81% impersonate technology vendors, targeting SSO, identity providers, and VPNs. SLH flips the convention: helpdesk-organization[.]com, sso-organization[.]com, ticket-organization[.]com. Pink and FALCON concentrate on the passkey theme (*passkey[.]com), register predominantly through NICENIC, and front with Cloudflare and DDoS-Guard. Critically, these domains are registered shortly before an intrusion and taken down immediately after, so real-time brand monitoring and new-domain alerting matter more than blocklists.
- Law enforcement has made meaningful progress but not stopped the ecosystem. Noah Urban became the first convicted Scattered Spider member in August 2025, receiving a 10-year US 🇺🇸 sentence and $13M restitution. A July 2026 DOJ complaint ties the Flowers/Jubair cluster to approximately 120 network intrusions, at least 47 US 🇺🇸 victims between May 2022 and September 2025, and over $115M in paid ransoms. Owen Flowers (18) and Thalha Jubair (20) were sentenced to 5.5 years each at Woolwich Crown Court for the Transport for London hack, which caused £29M in losses, took 148 systems offline, and forced 27,000 staff to reset passwords in person. Investigators correlated physical SIM-swapping hardware to suspects and tracked Telegram handles back to real identities. BreachForums was seized by US 🇺🇸 and French 🇫🇷 law enforcement in October 2025 following public extortion campaigns against Salesforce.
- The defensive priority is identity hardening, not perimeter controls. These groups win by abusing valid credentials and help-desk processes, not by finding unpatched services. Phishing-resistant FIDO2 or passkey MFA eliminates SIM-swap and MFA bombing paths. Help desks must verify caller identity independently before any password reset or MFA device enrollment. OAuth and connected-app scopes should be audited regularly, secrets must leave documentation and move into secrets managers, and bulk-export monitoring on SharePoint, OneDrive, Box, and Salesforce should be active. Monitor for new domain registrations containing your organization name or brand terms: attacker infrastructure appears and disappears within the intrusion window.
Practitioner takeaway: hunt your identity logs first. Look for new MFA device registrations, Okta and Azure AD policy changes, OAuth application grants, and help-desk ticket activity preceding any privilege escalation. Cross-reference against newly registered lookalike domains using the wildcard patterns in the report (*-sso[.]com, *-okta[.]com, *-helpdesk[.]com, *passkey[.]com, and the SLH inverse formats). The full IOC patterns, TTP matrix, and domain query examples are in the Pulsedive report.

item.title: Defending Against Active Exploitation of Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway Appliances
item.description:
Two zero-days actively exploited in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway since early September 2026, with government, financial, education, and legal sectors in North America and Europe targeted.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88772 is the primary zero-day: a pre-authentication heap corruption flaw in the NetScaler Packet Processing Engine (NSPPE) triggered over DTLS on UDP/443. Malformed DTLS record headers corrupt memory and redirect code execution to root-level shellcode on the underlying FreeBSD platform. Exploitation leaves two distinct log artifacts: an SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE event with ClientVersion DTLSv1.0 and reason "Handshake failure-Internal Error" in syslog, followed by NSPPE process termination messages from the pitboss watchdog in /var/log/messages. A DTLS failure followed within minutes by an NSPPE crash on the same appliance is Mandiant's strongest exploitation signal. CVE-2026-88771 is a second zero-day being actively exploited per vendor disclosure; the compensating controls for CVE-2026-88772 (disabling DTLS, blocking UDP/443) do not mitigate it.
- Post-exploitation persistence is achieved by modifying /etc/httpd.conf to treat non-PHP extensions as executable PHP scripts. Two variants were observed: registering .deb files as PHP handlers with web shells staged in /netscaler/gui/vpn/scripts/linux, and a stealthier AliasMatch directive that maps HTTP requests for /vpn/media/*.ico to corresponding .sig files in the same directory. The setuid bit is then asserted on /bin/sh (chmod u+s /bin/sh) to give the unprivileged web server process persistent root execution. The installer triggers a full appliance reboot via /netscaler/nsshutdown -R to apply changes.
- Two novel malware families anchor the post-exploitation toolkit. WHIPSHOT is a PHP web shell disguised as a Debian package in /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/scripts/linux/. It reads C2 commands from chunked HTTP headers (HTTP_X_UX_0 through HTTP_X_UX_95), Base64-decodes the stream, and forwards it over loopback to SLAPSHOT. It returns a spoofed HTTP 404 while embedding tunneled responses in the body. SLAPSHOT is a Python TCP tunneler that binds to an ephemeral loopback port, writes it to /tmp/.uxdport, and uses fcntl.flock on /tmp/.uxdlock to enforce a single instance. It speaks a custom binary protocol (4-byte big-endian length prefix plus JSON) supporting open, push, pull, exch, close, and ping actions. SLAPSHOT self-terminates after 10 minutes of idle to reduce its memory footprint. Other standalone installer shells extract Base64-encoded commands from native NetScaler headers HTTP_NSC_LDAP and HTTP_NSC_CLIENTTYPE, executing via eval() while returning HTTP 404 and scrubbing their paths from /etc/crontab with a regex wiper.
- Key forensic hunt steps: check /etc/httpd.conf for AddHandler application/x-httpd-php on non-.php extensions and AliasMatch directives pointing /vpn/media/ or /vpn/theme/ to script directories. Run "file" and grep for PHP markers across /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/scripts/linux/, /var/netscaler/gui/vpns/scripts/vista/, /var/netscaler/gui/vpns/scripts/mac/, and /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/media/. Check ls -l /bin/sh for -rwsr-xr-x with root ownership. Inspect /tmp/ for .uxdport and .uxdlock. Review httperror logs for .sig or .deb execution errors that persist even after access logs are wiped, and httpaccess.log for 404 responses to .ico paths returning bodies over 5KB. Review /var/log/sh.log for nsshutdown -R and httpd -k restart commands outside change windows.
Practitioner takeaway: Patch to NetScaler 14.1-73.37 or 13.1-64.23 immediately. If you cannot patch, disable DTLS and block inbound UDP/443 upstream of the appliance (not via local ACL, which still lets traffic reach the vulnerable NSPPE). For confirmed compromise, halt HA synchronization before validating the standby node to prevent replication of the malicious httpd.conf. Rotate all LDAP bind accounts, RADIUS secrets, TLS certificates, and private keys after patching, not before. The report includes a full IOC collection in GTI plus five YARA rules covering WHIPSHOT, SLAPSHOT, unauthorized httpd.conf directives, NSC header web shells, and persistence installers. Defenders should confirm that /var/log/messages and web server access and error logs are forwarded to SIEM, as they are not included in standard ns.log syslog forwarding and contain the primary exploitation evidence.

item.title: Here We Go Again (Citrix NetScaler DTLS Preauth Memory Overflow CVE-2026-88772)
item.description:
CVE-2026-88772: Citrix NetScaler DTLS preauth memory overflow reaches RCE via a 137,825-byte scratch buffer overwrite, exploited in the wild as a zero-day. No login required, DTLS on by default.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88772 carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5 Critical and was confirmed exploited in the wild before Citrix patched it in bulletin CTX697096. It is one of eight vulnerabilities fixed together, two of which (CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772) were actively exploited zero-days. DTLS must be enabled, which is the default on VPN virtual servers unless an admin explicitly set -dtls OFF. No authentication is required: the attacker only needs to complete a DTLS cookie exchange to prove their IP is reachable, then send 120 crafted records.
- The root cause is in nsppe, the core NetScaler binary. A function that stitches an NSB (NetScaler Buffer) chain into a fixed 0x8c00-byte (35,840-byte) scratch buffer in the .bss section calls memcpy in a loop with no bounds check. The patch (comparing r15d against edx before each memcpy and rejecting oversized chains) is visible in the diff between build 73.30 and 73.37. The overflow lands 173,665 bytes into a 35,840-byte region: 137,825 bytes of attacker-controlled data spill into adjacent writable nsppe memory.
- The exploit chain is fully preauth and walks a clean path to shellcode: craft 120 DTLS records where each claims fragment_length=1 of a 120-byte message but carries ~1,447 bytes of NSB data, triggering reassembly to mark the message complete while the NSB chain holds ~174 KB. The overflow first corrupts a global list pointer (constant 0x357f820 in 14.1-73.30, no PIE), then overwrites a fake vtable at 0x355c800 to hijack a periodic background-thread virtual call. Because nsppe has no PIE and no stack canary, fixed ROP gadgets (pop rdi/ret at 0x4e705d, etc.) chain a FreeBSD SYS_mprotect syscall (74) to mark the payload page RWX and hand off to shellcode.
- The appliance runs FreeBSD, carries No RELRO, no stack canary, and no PIE, meaning the 41 MB nsppe binary sits at a fixed base (0x400000) across all affected builds. The entire exploit is deterministic once the cookie exchange succeeds. watchTowr's proof-of-concept detection artifact generator sends 120 records totaling 176,640 bytes over 9462/UDP to confirm susceptibility.
- Fixed versions: NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.37 and later, 13.1-64.23 and later, 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.37 FIPS and later, 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.279 and later. Note that CVE-2026-88778 (predictable ISN) requires enabling Enhanced ISN Generation separately, the upgrade alone does not fix it.
Responder action: hunt your perimeter logs for large volumes of DTLS traffic to 9462/UDP from a single source, specifically 120-record bursts totaling roughly 176 KB, which is the artifact this exploit leaves in network captures. On the appliance itself, look for nsppe crash dumps or core files in /var/crash and check for unexpected processes spawned from nsppe after a SIGSEGV. If you cannot patch immediately, explicitly set -dtls OFF on VPN virtual servers to remove the attack surface. The watchTowr detection artifact generator and the full IOC list are available in the report on their GitHub.

It is one of eight vulnerabilities fixed together, two of which (CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772) were actively exploited zero-days. DTLS must be enabled, which is the default on VPN virtual servers unless an admin explicitly set -dtls OFF. No authentication is required: the attacker only needs to complete a DTLS cookie exchange to prove their IP is reachable, then send 120 crafted records.

- The root cause is in nsppe, the core NetScaler binary. A function that stitches an NSB (NetScaler Buffer) chain into a fixed 0x8c00-byte (35,840-byte) scratch buffer in the .bss section calls memcpy in a loop with no bounds check. The patch (comparing r15d against edx before each memcpy and rejecting oversized chains) is visible in the diff between build 73.30 and 73.37. The overflow lands 173,665 bytes into a 35,840-byte region: 137,825 bytes of attacker-controlled data spill into adjacent writable nsppe memory.

- The exploit chain is fully preauth and walks a clean path to shellcode: craft 120 DTLS records where each claims fragment_length=1 of a 120-byte message but carries ~1,447 bytes of NSB data, triggering reassembly to mark the message complete while the NSB chain holds ~174 KB. The overflow first corrupts a global list pointer (constant 0x357f820 in 14.1-73.30, no PIE), then overwrites a fake vtable at 0x355c800 to hijack a periodic background-thread virtual call. Because nsppe has no PIE and no stack canary, fixed ROP gadgets (pop rdi/ret at 0x4e705d, etc.) chain a FreeBSD SYS_mprotect syscall (74) to mark the payload page RWX and hand off to shellcode.

- The appliance runs FreeBSD, carries No RELRO, no stack canary, and no PIE, meaning the 41 MB nsppe binary sits at a fixed base (0x400000) across all affected builds. The entire exploit is deterministic once the cookie exchange succeeds. watchTowr's proof-of-concept detection artifact generator sends 120 records totaling 176,640 bytes over 9462/UDP to confirm susceptibility.

- Fixed versions: NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.37 and later, 13.1-64.23 and later, 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.37 FIPS and later, 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.279 and later. Note that CVE-2026-88778 (predictable ISN) requires enabling Enhanced ISN Generation separately, the upgrade alone does not fix it.

Responder action: hunt your perimeter logs for large volumes of DTLS traffic to 9462/UDP from a single source, specifically 120-record bursts totaling roughly 176 KB, which is the artifact this exploit leaves in network captures. On the appliance itself, look for nsppe crash dumps or core files in /var/crash and check for unexpected processes spawned from nsppe after a SIGSEGV. If you cannot patch immediately, explicitly set -dtls OFF on VPN virtual servers to remove the attack surface. The watchTowr detection artifact generator and the full IOC list are available in the report on their GitHub.

item.title: New THOR Detection Coverage for Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772
item.description:
Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 are actively exploited in the wild, with pre-disclosure exploitation observed by GreyNoise on September 24, three days before Citrix published bulletin CTX697096.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88771 is an unauthenticated command injection vulnerability affecting default NetScaler ADC and Gateway deployments. No special feature configuration is required for exposure. GreyNoise captured exploitation attempts before public disclosure and documented a post-exploitation chain involving privilege changes and installation of a hidden, password-protected PHP webshell. The webshell combines command pass-through with cookie decoding and was configured so CSS-looking request paths route to it, a deliberate evasion choice. CVE-2026-88772 is a DTLS memory overflow enabling remote code execution or denial of service, affecting systems with DTLS enabled including VPN virtual servers where DTLS has not been explicitly disabled.
- Nextron has released four detection rules in the THOR Preview channel covering this activity. LOG_SUSP_EXPL_CVE_2026_88771_Sep26 hunts exploitation traces in NetScaler log data by correlating process-failure messages with attacker-controlled log content and shell metacharacters from the command injection path. WEBSHELL_CSS_PassThrough_Sep26 detects the compact PHP webshell pattern by behavior rather than filename, which matters because the actor hid the file. EXPL_CVE_2026_88772_POC_Sep26 flags PoC-related artifacts, not live exploitation. A YAML IOC set (id: 99f5048e-e8f1-40cd-ba39-9877dc2c67e7) converts 12 filesystem checks from Citrix's own IOC scanner script into four file-rule definitions covering suspicious PHP and XHTML files in NetScaler web directories, unusual signature files, and specific package artifacts.
- The YAML IOC set deliberately excludes 22 checks from the Citrix scanner that depend on log content, process state, file ownership, or runtime context. Those conditions cannot be represented as file-path IOCs. Responders should treat the file-rule set as a triage layer, not a complete compromise determination. The path expressions are case-insensitive and support mounted-image prefixes, making them usable directly against forensic images or collected filesystem trees pulled from appliances.
- Because exploitation was observed before Citrix's September 27 public disclosure, patching alone does not answer the question of whether an appliance was already compromised during the exposure window. Organizations need a compromise assessment of any NetScaler ADC or Gateway system that was internet-exposed before the patch was applied, not just an update check.
Practitioner takeaway: preserve NetScaler logs and a full filesystem snapshot before patching. Run the THOR Preview signatures (thor-util update --sigdev) and the YAML IOC set against the collected evidence. Focus log review on process-failure messages correlated with shell metacharacters, and look for hidden files in NetScaler web directories with PHP or XHTML extensions. Citrix's fixed releases are documented in CTX697096. Nextron states Preview signatures will update daily as the situation develops, so pull fresh signatures before each scan run. Full IOC set and detection rules are in the report.

item.title: Attackers Abuse ChatGPT Custom GPTs to Deliver RAT via ClickFix
item.description:
Custom GPT lure funnels victims into an 8-stage ClickFix-to-RAT chain. Attackers paid for Google Ads to surface a fake ChatGPT model, then deployed DLL sideloading, steganography, and an encrypted custom file system to land a full-featured RAT with DNS-over-HTTPS C2.
Key findings:
- The lure chain starts with a Google-Ads-sponsored result pointing to attacker-created Custom GPTs titled "Plus 5.6" at hxxps://chatgpt[.]com/g/g-6ab595ad6554819181b686d4876efb80-plus-5-6 (taken down) and hxxps://chatgpt[.]com/g/g-6ab6ba039440819185ed491740b11cf8-plus-5-6 (still active at publication). The GPT serves a single scripted reply directing users to a Google Sites ClickFix page at hxxps://sites.google[.]com/view/antibot172881, where a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA prompts them to paste a PowerShell command. That command uses a decimal-form IP, 1614733393 resolving to 96.62.224[.]81, to evade dotted-IP detection rules, drops a GUID-named MSI from %TEMP%, then deletes itself.
- The MSI (ISOSimple.msi, SHA256: 6761aad48a3f987238994d92bca97e4b8550e0150607bd67b47b1b6366a371fc) installs silently to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Advanced Printer Configuration Reader\, hides from Programs and Features via ARPSYSTEMCOMPONENT=1, and abuses a legitimate Canon-signed COTFileReadApp.exe to sideload a patched ceiinfolog.dll (signature stripped, SHA256: e58831766e8d4313db9f8b85f90c3a840aa0d84cfeac285beefa40e39ad0d1fb). That patched DLL adds one import, rdCore.dll, so Windows loads the malicious chain the moment the Canon app loads its own logger. Persistence lands as both an HKCU Run value and a scheduled task, both named Canon Configuration Reader, both pointing back to COTFileReadApp.exe.
- The loader hides inside Common.Integrator.Preview.wav (SHA256: 54c94f85ba6e950903d5ff42c0971c5a9d0741596be26e06afe7d60ec38edf31). The RIFF/WAVE header claims roughly 700 KB; the real file is over 1 MB. At offset 0x24362, real audio samples give way to 341,395 bytes of ciphertext decrypted by a rolling XOR with two stirred counters. The resulting in-memory shellcode (SHA256: 20c7befc174a61117770535e809046c75e93c71284bf1a9c6cd532f55b315f53) runs AMSI bypass against amsi.dll, unhooks ntdll.dll to evade EDR hooks, hosts the .NET CLR v4.0.30319 in memory, and performs anti-VM checks against VMware, VirtualBox, Hyper-V, QEMU, Xen, and Parallels driver and service names before opening an encrypted custom archive, monitor.raw (SHA256: e614b7d5a7a363fb1b355a87e2e8d9e8a05bbbca08f2cee3d606bdb5015ac53b), which holds 315 folders, 806 files, a persistence script, and the final RAT shellcode.
- The RAT (SHA256: ab65bbfc505dbe1cebe6021fb36e2011f6aa1d64f5d87cee1cbee3fc2a0c7907) is full-featured: remote desktop, screen broadcast, camera and microphone capture, credential harvesting from 17 browsers, a file manager with full-content search, and a payload deployer that handles EXE, DLL, MSI, PowerShell, Batch, VBScript, JScript, and ZIP. C2 discovery uses DNS-over-HTTPS through Cloudflare, Google, and Quad9 resolvers, so C2 lookups never appear in local DNS logs. On investigated hosts the RAT dropped a legitimately signed GOMCam2024.exe to %LOCALAPPDATA%\AppstorageFile\ and launched chrome.exe with a throwaway profile from %TEMP%.
- A version 2 swap replaced Canon with Stardock's DeElevate64.exe and DeElevator64.dll, renamed persistence to "Stardock DeElevation Tool," and moved the loader from a WAV into a real Microsoft NuGet package, Build.dat (SHA256: d3fda1e6cf886fd530bf62e2d16c39ad23ed12a2c933fc211f1f4876ceaa033e). The RAT payload is byte-for-byte identical across both versions. A third MSI, UltraFreeISOCreateWizardSolution.msi, was observed on the same server on 2026-09-23, confirming the signed-host costume rotation is ongoing.
Hunt for behavior, not names: detect PowerShell spawning msiexec on a GUID-named MSI in %TEMP%, any signed binary launched by msiexec from a non-standard %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ subdirectory, and HKCU Run values or scheduled tasks that reappear within minutes of deletion. Before removing persistence, kill the parent process first or the embedded script will restore both within 150-875 seconds. When investigating, check for unsigned DLLs alongside the signed host binary, and audit outbound HTTPS to Cloudflare, Google, and Quad9 resolvers for C2 lookups masquerading as ordinary DoH traffic. The full IOC table and file hashes are in the Huntress report.

item.title: From KMS Auto to Scareware: Tracking a Multi-Stage Intrusion Linked to APT36?
item.description:
A cracked KMS activation tool seeds a multi-day intrusion chain ending in APT36-branded scareware, with XMRig, ScreenConnect, and MeshAgent deployed as stepping stones across 12-24 hour intervals.
Key findings:
- KMS Auto executed from an untrusted source served as the initial access vector (T1204.002). What looked like a routine software activation event was the entry point for a staged compromise. The critical forensic tell is not the tool itself but where it ran from and what child processes followed. Execution from unusual directories with subsequent miner or RAT activity should immediately escalate triage priority.
- XMRig deployed post-compromise for cryptocurrency mining (T1496), followed hours later by ScreenConnect dropped to C:\ProgramData\HvHosts\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe and C:\ProgramData\OneDriveServer\OneDriveServer\OneDriveServer\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe. MeshAgent was then added as a redundant backdoor. The consistent 12-24 hour staging interval between each capability drop is a behavioral signature worth hunting across endpoint telemetry.
- The final payload, SecurityHealthServices.exe, masquerades as a Windows Defender process (T1036.005) and lands in %ProgramData%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup for persistence (T1547.001). It carries APT36 and Transparent Tribe Pakistan 🇵🇰 branding in its metadata and icon, changes the desktop wallpaper to a Pakistani 🇵🇰 flag, and throws a locked overlay screen. Despite the ransomware theater, no file encryption occurs. It appends a second .exe extension to filenames and drops self-copies with super-hidden attributes into AppData (T1564.001). The ransom note contains no wallet address, no payment deadline, and no contact channel, which is the clearest indicator this is scareware, not ransomware.
- Attribution to APT36 (Transparent Tribe, Mythic Leopard, COPPER FIELDSTONE) is not confirmed by K7 Labs. The metadata and branding could be planted misdirection. The overall pattern, a home user hit by a cracked tool leading to a mining and RMM chain capped with a psychological payload, does not match APT36's known surgical espionage tradecraft against military and diplomatic targets. Treat the APT36 label as an artifact of the payload, not a confirmed attribution.
- Five hashes are listed in the IOC table: three Trojan detections tied to the scareware payload, one CryptoMiner detection for the XMRig component, and one RemoteTool detection for ScreenConnect. Full IOC list is in the report.
Hunt for the staging pattern: KMSAuto execution outside system directories, followed within 24 hours by XMRig process creation, then ScreenConnect or MeshAgent installation, then a new Startup folder entry named SecurityHealthServices.exe. Cross-reference Run and RunOnce registry keys and the C:\Users\Public\Recovery path for dropped batch scripts, VBS files, and XML configs. The double-.exe extension rename on non-encrypted files is a low-cost sweep for active scareware infections. Full IOC list is in the K7 Labs report.

item.title: CLOSEDQUORUM: Malware Puts AI in the C2 Loop
item.description:
CLOSEDQUORUM is the first publicly documented Windows implant to replace human C2 tasking with a commercial LLM voting panel, delegating tactical attack decisions to DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini in sequence.
Key findings:
- The implant is a 16.4 MB, 64-bit Go executable discovered by Cisco Talos through its CAIRN project. At initialization it collects hostname, OS architecture, CPU count, Windows version, privilege status, and current target process, then sends that host context to up to four LLM providers. Each model returns a structured JSON response selecting the next action. Plurality vote wins. Ties resolve deterministically by provider order: DeepSeek, then Qwen, then Mistral, then Gemini. If all providers fail, the implant sleeps and retries rather than defaulting to a capability.
- The LLM decision layer selects from a constrained action set. "steal" triggers simultaneous LSASS credential dumping, saved credential theft from Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and cryptocurrency wallet theft from MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum stores. Stolen data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and exfiltrated via Discord webhook. "inject" invokes shellcode and routes to either process hollowing or Early Bird APC injection. "persist" invokes persistence routines, and Talos identifies WMI persistence creation as a correlatable behavior. A "move" decision exists in the schema but has no implemented handler in the analyzed build.
- The publicly distributed binary is an inert template with placeholder LLM API keys and a dummy Discord webhook. Talos assesses the operating model as a configurable service: operators compile a custom build with their own credentials before deployment, and stolen credentials flow back through their Discord channel, effectively a credentials-as-a-service offering with autonomous LLM orchestration as the differentiator. Developer artifacts link to criminal-forum carding activity dating to 2025. No confirmed in-the-wild deployment has been observed.
- The architectural significance is the effort displacement model. The LLMs are not writing exploits or inventing attack paths. They are choosing among predefined capabilities the developer already coded, using host context as input. This removes the human operator from a bounded decision loop and allows the implant to continue executing while the attacker is offline. The same pattern is extensible to other intrusion phases, and it routes all C2 traffic through legitimate commercial AI infrastructure rather than attacker-controlled domains or IPs, putting pressure on detections that depend on known-bad destinations.
Six SHA-256 hashes are listed in the report: 250d4fa37488af9b025333fa17705573d721467b203765bc360890b4f5a90cd7, c4dc171f2513fcaf9d5ecc815a94aee4063b213ab380f80bd3ac422dee5205a7, c13cea04f598e2b0c248d603a6e31bd13aabb64d8149c1b6a77b64e0b983a86f, f5f1f8c3e7b883793800ab6ccf21b3e60bd0730f300b4595fe74a33adc17a63c, 5191cf625dfc209a347f137b50aea199e82040fd5ee9086fb3e2de73c133f3cb, and eddbd0ecf7195d38fefae5b9d393abfa79e6f3f94bde19308ecef130a05a42e5.
Hunt for Go-compiled 64-bit executables making outbound HTTPS to LLM provider API endpoints alongside concurrent Discord webhook POST traffic. Correlate with LSASS access events, WMI subscription creation, and process hollowing indicators such as a spawned suspended process followed by WriteProcessMemory and ResumeThread calls. Wallet and browser credential paths in AppData are the on-disk artifacts to triage. The implant's LLM dependency also means API key strings embedded in a binary are a detection surface worth adding to your triage playbook.

item.title: Detections Digest #20260928
item.description:
Weekly detection engineering roundup: 80 new rules and 43 updates across 11 repositories cover RMM abuse, LSASS dumping, email evasion, BYOVD, and Kubernetes container threats from Sep 21-28, 2026.
Key findings this week:
- RMM abuse detection expanded significantly via magicsword-io/LOLRMM and RussianPanda95/Yara-Rules, with 41 new rules covering process creation, file artifacts, registry persistence under Run keys and service installation paths, and outbound network connections for tools including Zecurit, Allocentra, OpenDesk, RMMCRAT, BlackCrypt, LightRmmAgent, and RemoteAgentAgent. A new YARA rule for RMMCRAT specifically targets PE headers combined with embedded RMMC and RMM Agent configuration strings. The generic DNS rule covering known RMM infrastructure was also refreshed with updated domain and IP indicators. Hunt for agent binaries in AppData, ProgramData, and Program Files alongside Run key writes and outbound DNS to unfamiliar cloud hosting endpoints.
- LSASS and token access detections in splunk/security_content and SigmaHQ/sigma moved from static GrantedAccess string matching to bitwise evaluations against Sysmon Event ID 10 telemetry. This matters because minor mask variations broke prior rules. Updated rules now cover read permissions on lsass.exe, Winlogon duplicate handle access, WMI token impersonation via wmiprvse.exe, and injection into notepad.exe. The Dumpert LSASS dumper detection shifted to IMPHASH-based matching rather than MD5 or command-line paths, which are trivially modified. Cross-reference Sysmon Event ID 10 bitwise access masks with process lineage and file_path fields for Task Manager dump artifacts.
- Email evasion coverage in sublime-security/sublime-rules received 12 new and 12 updated rules. New detections parse .ics calendar invites with oversized guest lists carrying voicemail, purchase order, missed call, and BEC lures, and decode hex-obfuscated recipient strings embedded in URL fragments and QR codes across PDF, ICS, and image attachments. Rules also flag Google Cloud Storage links to short HTML paths, newly registered domains on suspicious TLDs serving single-character HTML files, client-side JavaScript beaconing visitor tokens via dynamic Image objects, and Teams help desk impersonation correlated with mail bombing within a one-hour window. Updated rules unwrap Mimecast-protected links and refresh Spamhaus ASN-DROP coverage, removing prefixes tied to AS63023 and AS62563.
- BYOVD and in-memory defense evasion coverage updated across magicsword-io/LOLDrivers, rabbitstack/fibratus, and kevoreilly/CAPEv2. LOLDrivers rules added MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH values alongside driver filenames in ImageLoaded telemetry to catch hypervisor-protected code integrity bypasses. Four Fibratus rules for process hollowing, ghostly hollowing, activation context manipulation, and NTDLL remapping via file mapping were updated for engine version 3.2.0, refining section type filters including IMAGE and IMAGE_NO_EXECUTE. A new YARA rule in CAPEv2 detects Defendnot, a tool that impairs Windows Defender, via PE magic bytes and characteristic debug strings.
- Kubernetes container threat detection expanded through benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting with 13 new KQL rules querying CloudProcessEvents and CloudAuditEvents in Microsoft Defender XDR. Coverage includes reverse shells using network redirection, XMRig and Kinsing cryptominer execution, first-seen container binary baselining, container escape via nsenter, chroot, unshare, and socket interaction, service account token and ca.crt file reads, Kubernetes secret enumeration across namespaces, cluster-admin role binding creation, and deployment from unapproved registries. GitOps controllers ArgoCD and Flux are excluded to reduce noise. A new jkerai1 rule monitors AzureActivity for modifications to Azure public and private DNS zones, a low-visibility path adversaries use for traffic redirection.
Practitioner takeaway: the shift from static hash and string matching to bitwise access mask evaluation in LSASS rules is the most operationally significant change this week, since it closes a known evasion gap. Prioritize pulling updated Sysmon Event ID 10 rules from splunk/security_content and SigmaHQ/sigma into your pipeline. For RMM hunting, stack process, file path, registry, and network rules together rather than running them in isolation: a single layer is easy to miss, four correlated layers is a detection story. Full rule sets, IOCs, and YARA content are available in the linked repositories.
